chunks.contentMarkdown:
### A. *Introduction to the Mitzvah of Challah*

Bez”H, this *zman* we will learn about *mitzvos* that pertain to *Eretz Yisrael*, specifically the *mitzvos* of *hafrashas challah* and *terumos u’maasros.* While these *mitzvos* are rooted in the *kedusha* of the Land and are thus called *mitzvos hateluyos ba’aretz*, we will see that *hafrashas challah* applies even in *chutz la’aretz*, and there are numerous practical situations in which *terumos u’maasros* may also apply even outside of *Eretz Yisrael*. The importance of these *mitzvos* can be seen from Chazal.  The **גמרא סוטה** (יד.) explains that Moshe Rabbeinu longed to enter *Eretz* *Yisrael* so that he would have the opportunity to fulfill the *mitzvos* that are dependent upon the Land*.* Today, we are blessed with millions of Jews living in and visiting Eretz Yisrael, and we all hope and believe the coming of *Mashiach* is imminent. Therefore, these *halachos* are especially relevant, whether you live in *Eretz Yisrael* or not. 

We will spend the majority of the *zman* learning the *halachos* of *hafrashas challah,* a *mitzvah* that applies throughout the world and about which the Midrash in **בראשית רבה** פ״א-א teaches that the world was created in its merit. In this introductory section, we will discuss whether the obligation of *hafrashas challah* is biblical or rabbinic.

chunks.summary: The Torah obligation to give the first portion of dough to a kohen; challah is called terumah and the dough is tevel until separated.
chunks.sectionTitle: Introduction to the Mitzvah of Challah

blocks.text: In במדבר (טו:יז-כא) (1), the Torah teaches that when the Jewish people enter the Land of Israel, anyone who bakes is obligated to give the first portion of the dough to a kohen. The Torah refers to hafrashas challah as “terumah,” and we will learn below that according to some customs, the word “terumah” is included in the bracha of hafrashas challah.[1] Thus, when one prepares a batch of dough (of an amount which will be discussed below), the dough has the status of טבל (similar to produce from which teruma and ma’aasros were not yet taken). Only after the challah is separated does the dough become permissible.[2]

Only after the *challah* is separated does the dough become permissible.[2]

chunks.summary: Rashi/Sifrei: unlike other mitzvos hateluyos ba’aretz, challah began immediately when Klal Yisrael entered Eretz Yisrael.

blocks.text: Rashi quotes the ספרי, which teaches that regarding all other mitzvos that apply in Eretz Yisrael, the Torah uses the language of ״כי תבוא״ or ״כי תבאו״, which teaches us that the mitzvah only begins after the Land is conquered and settled, a process that took Yehoshua fourteen after crossing the Jordan River. In contrast, regarding challah, the Torah uses the expression ״בבואכם״ – “when you enter,” teaching that the mitzvah took effect as soon as the Jewish people entered the land, even before it was fully conquered and settled.

chunks.title: Gemara Kesubos: Biblical or Rabbinic Today
chunks.summary: Machlokes in Gemara; Rambam and S”A that today even in Eretz Yisrael is rabbinic unless the Jewish people are living there; chu”l enacted so challah is not forgotten.
chunks.sectionTitle: Introduction to the Mitzvah of Challah

blocks.text: The גמרא כתובות (כה.) (2) quotes a dispute whether the mitzvah of hafrashas challah today is biblical or rabbinic. The students of Rav maintain that even the opinions who hold that terumah today is only rabbinic agree that the mitzvah of challah is biblical because, as mentioned above, it took effect the moment the Jewish people entered Eretz Yisrael and was not dependent upon conquering the Land. רב הונא argues that even according to the opinions that terumah today is biblical, the mitzvah of hafrashas challah is only rabbinic. Since the Torah writes ״בבואכם״ – implying that everyone needs to enter the land, the mitzvah of challah is rabbinic when most Jews no longer live there. This was true already in the time of Ezra, when although many Jews returned to Eretz Yisrael, the majority of Jews stayed behind (see Rashi).

chunks.contentMarkdown:
The **גמרא כתובות** (כה.) (2) quotes a dispute whether the *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah* today is biblical or rabbinic. The students of Rav maintain that even the opinions who hold that *terumah* today is only rabbinic agree that the *mitzvah* of *challah* is biblical because, as mentioned above, it took effect the moment the Jewish people entered *Eretz Yisrael* and was not dependent upon conquering the Land. רב הונא argues that even according to the opinions that *terumah* today is biblical, the *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah* is only rabbinic. Since the Torah writes ״בבואכם״ – implying that **everyone** needs to enter the land, the *mitzvah* of *challah* is rabbinic when most Jews no longer live there. This was true already in the time of Ezra, when although many Jews returned to *Eretz Yisrael,* the **majority** of Jews stayed behind (see Rashi). 

The **רמב״ם** (ספר המצות קלג) lists the *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah* as the 133rd *mitzvah* in his *minyan ha’mitzvos*. In **הלכות** **ביכורים** (פ״ה-ה) (3), the רמב״ם *passkins* like רב הונא that the biblical obligation of *hafrashas challah* only applies in *Eretz Yisrael* when **all****[3]** of the Jews are living there. He quotes רב הונא’s statement in the above Gemara that even in the time of Ezra, the *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah* was only rabbinic since the majority of Jews remained behind in Bavel. The רמב״ם adds in הלכה ז׳ that Chazal enacted a *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah* in *chutz la’aretz* in order to ensure that the *mitzvah* of *challah* should not be forgotten (see בכורות כז.).

The S”A in the beginning of **סימן שכב-א** *passkins* that there is a **biblical** *mitzvah* to separate a portion of your dough and give it to a *kohen.* In **סעיף ב׳**, he *passkins* like the above רמב״ם that today, even in *Eretz* *Yisrael* the *mitzvah* is only **rabbinic** because the biblical *mitzvah* applies only when **all** Jews are living in Israel. In **סעיף ג׳** he adds that there is a rabbinic *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah* in *chutz la’aretz* in order that the mitzvah should not be forgotten.[4]

Source Notes

[3]:  We will discuss below if this means all Jews or the majority of Jews.

[4]:  Why did Chazal not enact a similar rabbinic *mitzvah* of *terumah* on fruits and vegetables in *chutz la’aretz* in order that it should not be forgotten? The רמב״ן (הוספות בסוף יבמות) explains that *terumah* only applies to farmers, so we are not worried it would be forgotten, but since everyone prepares bread at home, if there was no *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah,* it might be forgotten. The יראים (קמח) explains that since flour that is brought from *chutz la’aretz* and made into dough in *Eretz Yisrael* is obligated in *challah,* Chazal required being *mafrish challah* on all doughs.

chunks.title: Current Demographics and the Question Today
chunks.summary: Raises the possibility that the majority of Jews may live in Eretz Yisrael and asks whether that changes challah, shemittah, and terumah.
chunks.sectionTitle: Status of Hafrashas Challah Today

blocks.text: Status of Hafrashas Challah Today

Given what we have learned so far in the previous section, the next question that must be asked is what is the halachic status of the mitzvah of challah today in Eretz Yisrael? As mentioned above, Rashi to the גמרא כתובות (2) implies that when the majority of Jews reside in Eretz Yisrael, the mitzvah of hafrashas challah is biblical, which would have practical implications as well, such as requiring us to rule stringently about any safek that arises. As of 2026, there are about 7.3 million Jews living in Israel and 8.5 million Jews living outside of Israel.[5] From the 8.5 million living outside of Israel, 37% in the US are Reform, many of whom were converted or born to a mother converted through the Reform movement, which would render them not halachically Jewish. Therefore, it stands to reason that even today, the majority of Jews in the world already reside in Israel. Even if these figures are not precise, in the next few years, it nevertheless appears likely that a majority of Jews will be living in Israel for the first time since the first Beis Ha’Mikdash.

### B. *Status of Hafrashas Challah Today*

Given what we have learned so far in the previous section, the next question that must be asked is what is the *halachic* status of the *mitzvah* of *challah* today in *Eretz Yisrael*? As mentioned above, Rashi to the גמרא כתובות (2) implies that when the majority of Jews reside in *Eretz Yisrael*, the *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah* is biblical, which would have practical implications as well, such as requiring us to rule stringently about any *safek* that arises. As of 2026, there are about 7.3 million Jews living in Israel and 8.5 million Jews living outside of Israel.[5] From the 8.5 million living outside of Israel, 37% in the US are Reform, many of whom were converted or born to a mother converted through the Reform movement, which would render them not *halachically* Jewish. Therefore, it stands to reason that even today, the majority of Jews in the world already reside in Israel. Even if these figures are not precise, in the next few years, it nevertheless appears likely that a majority of Jews will be living in Israel for the first time since the first Beis Ha’Mikdash.

Furthermore, if we are to assume that the majority of Jews today are living in Israel (or if this will happen in the next few years), we must consider whether this affects the *halachic* status of *shemittah* and *terumah* as well as *challah*. One of the major leniencies relied upon by the *Rabbanut* in Israel during the *shemittah* year to permit the land to be worked is the ״היתר מכירה״ – selling the land to non-Jews. Bez”H, in a future SCP-*zman* we will discuss the details of this *kula* and whether it is a reliable one, but those who rely on the *kula* do so in part because *shemittah* today is rabbinic. If, however, by the next *shemittah* year, the majority of Jews would reside in Israel, would that abolish the validity of the *heter mechirah*? 

We will begin by discussing whether the *mitzvah* of *shemittah* becomes biblical when the majority of Jews reside in Israel. We will then examine the status of *challah* and *terumah* today.

chunks.title: Shemittah Today and Yovel
chunks.summary: Rambam: shemittah is biblical only when yovel applies, which requires Jews settled by shevet; therefore likely rabbinic until Mashiach.
chunks.sectionTitle: Status of Hafrashas Challah Today

blocks.text: I. Shemittah today

Regarding shemittah, the רמב״ם (הלכות שמיטה ויובל פ״י-ח) (4) passkins that shemittah is biblically mandated only when yovel (the 50th year, in which real estate that was sold returns to its  original owner and Jewish slaves are freed) is also in effect. However, yovel applies only when all (or at least the majority) of the Jews reside in their ancestral portion of the Land according to their shevet. Today, when most Jews do not know what shevet they belong to and are certainly not settled in their designated plot of land, yovel does not apply. Consequently, shemittah remains rabbinic in nature. Therefore, even if all the Jews were to return and live in Eretz Yisrael, shemittah would remain rabbinic until the coming of Mashiach, who will identify each tribe and restore every shevet to its designated portion of the Land.[6]

Regarding *shemittah,* the **רמב״ם** (הלכות שמיטה ויובל פ״י-ח) (4) *passkins* that *shemittah* is biblically mandated only when *yovel* (the 50th year, in which real estate that was sold returns to its  original owner and Jewish slaves are freed) is also in effect. However, *yovel* applies only when all (or at least the majority) of the Jews reside in their ancestral portion of the Land according to their *shevet*. Consequently, *shemittah* remains rabbinic in nature. Therefore, even if all the Jews were to return and live in *Eretz Yisrael*, *shemittah* would remain rabbinic until the coming of *Mashiach*, who will identify each tribe and restore every *shevet* to its designated portion of the Land.[6]

chunks.title: Challah Today — Majority of Jews in Eretz Yisrael
chunks.summary: Ritva and Be’er Basadeh say majority suffices; Chazon Ish suggests entry may need Hashem’s direction through king or Navi.
chunks.sectionTitle: Status of Hafrashas Challah Today

blocks.text: II. Challah today

Regarding challah, there is a dispute whether the mitzvah becomes biblical when the majority of Jews return to Eretz Yisrael. As opposed to Shemittah, challah is not connected to yovel. Rather, it became obligatory immediately after the Jewish nation entered Eretz Yisrael, even before the Land had been conquered and settled. Therefore, it would seem that the moment the majority of Jews enter Israel, even if the land isn’t officially conquered, the mitzvah should once again become biblical. In fact, the ריטב״א (כתובות כה. ד״ה בבואכם) (5) passkins that as soon as the majority of Jews reside in Israel, the mitzvah of challah in Eretz Yisrael becomes biblical again.

chunks.contentMarkdown:
<u>II.</u> *<u>Challah</u>* <u>today</u>

Regarding *challah,* there is a dispute whether the *mitzvah* becomes biblical when the majority of Jews return to *Eretz Yisrael.* As opposed to *Shemittah, challah* is not connected to *yovel.* Rather, it became obligatory immediately after the Jewish nation entered *Eretz Yisrael,* even before the Land had been conquered and settled. Therefore, it would seem that the moment the majority of Jews enter Israel, even if the land isn’t officially conquered, the *mitzvah* should once again become biblical. In fact, the **ריטב״א** (כתובות כה. ד״ה בבואכם) (5) *passkins* that as soon as the majority of Jews reside in Israel, the *mitzvah* of *challah* in *Eretz Yisrael* becomes biblical again.

Furthermore, even though the רמב״ם and S”A write that “all” Jews must return to the Land for the *mitzvah* to regain its biblical status, the **באר בשדה** (פ״א הע׳ ג) (6) maintains that the רמב״ם would agree that even a majority suffices. He explains that when עם ישראל initially conquered the land in the times of יהושע, not all of the Jews entered Israel, since the *shevatim* of Gad, Reuven, and half of Menashe stayed on the other side of the Jordan river. Granted, the men entered the land to fight, but that was only the fighting men ages 20-60, and even in that age group some stayed behind to protect the women and children who did not enter. Thus, even when the *mitzvah* of *challah* initially took effect, only the majority of Jews were in Israel, and at that moment in time, everyone agrees the *mitzvah* was biblical, so too, in our time, the *mitzvah* will become biblical the moment the majority of Jews reside in Israel. 

However, the **חזון איש** (שביעית כא-ה) (7) argues that even if the majority of Jews come to Israel, *challah* may nevertheless remain rabbinic, since the biblical obligation only goes into effect when two conditions are met: 1) the Jewish people enter the land under direction of a King or Navi, similar to when we entered the land of Israel the first time with יהושע. The **חלת לחם** (ס״א שירי ברכה-ה) suggests[7] that since with regard to *challah* the Torah commands ״אשר **אני** מביא אתכם שמה״ – “Where **I** am bringing you there,” that implies that the biblical *mitzvah* only goes into effect when the Jewish people enter with Hashem’s explicit direction (i.e., via a Navi or King). 2) The majority of Jews reside in the land. Today, only the second condition may be fulfilled, so the *mitzvah* would remain rabbinic. The חזון איש does entertain the possibility that the *mitzvah* may become biblical even without a king or Navi, but he ultimately appears to reject that.

To summarize, it seems from the ריטב״א and the באר בשדה that the *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah* becomes biblical as soon as the majority of Jews reside in *Eretz Yisrael* (which may already have occurred). The חזון איש, however, suggests that the *mitzvah* might remain rabbinic until we enter the Land under the direction of a King or Navi.

Source Notes

[7]:  Written by Rav Simcha Yoel Rubinstein (passed away in 1863), who was a Rav and *dayan* in Boberka, Ukraine.

Regarding terumah, the רמב״ם (תרומות פ״א-כו) (8) equates its status with that of challah, that separating terumah will only be biblical once the majority of Jews are living in the Land. The ראב״ד disagrees, maintaining that terumah is not equated to challah and the mitzvah today is biblical even if the majority of Jews are not living in the land. The S”A in סימן שלא-ב passkins like the רמב״ם. Although the Rama quotes the ראב״ד, he agrees lema’aseh with the pssak of the S”A that terumah is only rabbinic today. Based on what we learned regarding challah, one would think that according to the ריטב״א and באר בשדה, the mitzvah of terumah would also become biblical once the majority of Jews reside in the Land, whereas the חזון איש would argue that it would remain rabbinic. In truth, however, the חזון איש (שביעית כא-ה) (9) differentiates between challah and terumah, suggesting that the רמב״ם agrees that if the majority of Jews return to Eretz Yisrael, the mitzvah of terumah becomes biblical.

<u>III.</u> *<u>Terumah</u>* <u>today</u>

Regarding *terumah,* the **רמב״ם** (תרומות פ״א-כו) (8) equates its status with that of *challah*, that separating *terumah* will only be biblical once the majority of Jews are living in the Land. The **ראב״ד** disagrees, maintaining that *terumah* is not equated to *challah* and the *mitzvah* today is biblical even if the majority of Jews are not living in the land. The S”A in **סימן שלא-ב** *passkins* like the רמב״ם. Although the *Rama* quotes the ראב״ד, he agrees *lema’aseh* with the *pssak* of the S”A that *terumah* is only rabbinic today. Based on what we learned regarding *challah,* one would think that according to the ריטב״א and באר בשדה, the *mitzvah* of *terumah* would also become biblical once the majority of Jews reside in the Land, whereas the חזון איש would argue that it would remain rabbinic. In truth, however, the **חזון איש** (שביעית כא-ה) (9) differentiates between *challah* and *terumah,* suggesting that the רמב״ם agrees that if the majority of Jews return to *Eretz* *Yisrael*, the *mitzvah* of *terumah* becomes biblical. 

The חזון איש explains that although the condition of entering the Land under the direction of a king or *navi* may be needed regarding *challah,* this is not the case with regard to *terumah*. Nevertheless, two conditions are still necessary for *terumah* to become biblical: 1) The Land is sanctified, 2) the majority of Jews live in the Land. When Ezra returned to *Eretz Yisrael* before the second *Beis Hamikdash* was built, he sanctified the Land a second time, so the first condition has already been fulfilled.[8] Therefore, as soon as the majority of Jews live in *Eretz Yisrael*, *terumah* becomes biblical, even if *Mashiach* has not yet arrived. 

What emerges from here is that as soon as the majority of Jews live in Israel, a milestone that may have already been reached or will likely be reached in the near future, all will agree that the *mitzvah* of *terumah* becomes biblical. This would significantly increase the severity of the *mitzvah* and the importance of ensuring that it is performed properly. Therefore, when purchasing fruits or vegetables grown in *Eretz Yisrael,* one should make sure that the store has a reliable *hechsher,* or know how to properly be *mafrish terumos u’maasros* oneself.

Nevertheless, it is still possible that *terumah* will remain rabbinic for the foreseeable future. **Rav Chaim Kanievsky** in דרך אמונה (תרומות פ״א-כו בה״ל ד״ה וכן) (10) suggests that since the ten tribes are still lost, the majority of the Jews may still not reside in Israel. Furthermore, we may add that even without considering the lost tribes, accurately determining the world’s Jewish population is extremely difficult because if a Jewish woman becomes unaffiliated, her daughters and all future female descendants remain Jewish, but they are unaccounted for whenever a census is conducted. Similarly, in the world-wide census, many are counted as Jewish, even though their father alone is Jewish, and they are *halachically* defined as non-Jews.

Source Notes

[8]:  There is a dispute in the גמרא יבמות (פב:) whether this sanctification was nullified with the destruction of the second *Beis Ha’Mikdash* (קדושה שניה קידשה לשעתה או לעתיד לבוא), and the רמב״ם *passkins* like the opinion that the sanctification of the land of Israel by Ezra was eternal.

To summarize:

- There is a biblical *mitzvah* to give a portion of one’s dough to a *kohen.*

- The biblical *mitzvah* only applies in Eretz Yisrael, and only when the majority of Jews reside there; otherwise, the obligation is rabbinic.

  - Today, if the majority of Jews are already living in *Eretz Yisrael* (or if this occurs in the near future), some say the *mitzvah* is biblical. But the חזון איש suggests that it may remain rabbinic because perhaps the land needs to be entered by Hashem’s direction, via a king or Navi.

- The *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah* applies rabbinically in *chutz la’aretz* so that it should not be forgotten*.*

- The biblical obligation of *shemittah* will only go into effect when the land is settled based on the *shevatim* and *yovel* applies once again*.*

- According to many *Rishonim* (the ראב״ד and טור), the *mitzvah* of *teruma* today is biblical, though the S”A *passkins* like the רמב״ם that it is rabbinic.

  - The חזון איש agrees regarding *teruma* that if the majority of Jews return to Israel, the *mitzvah* of *teruma* will again become biblical.

  - R. Chaim Kanievsky suggests that the status of “majority of Jews living in Israel” might be dependent on the return of the 10 lost tribes.

blocks.text: We learned above that the majority of posskim maintain that the mitzvah of hafrashas challah, both in Eretz Yisrael and in chutz la’aretz, is currently rabbinic in nature. Nevertheless, there are a few situations in which the posskim are more machmir concerning challah in Eretz Yisrael than concerning challah in chutz la’aretz. The reason for this distinction is that the mitzvah of hafrashas challah in Eretz Yisrael is fundamentally biblical in nature, and is only rabbinic today because the majority of Jews do not currently reside in Israel. In contrast, the rabbinic mitzvah of hafrashas challah in chutz la’aretz was only enacted so that it would not be forgotten. We will list three practical distinctions between challah in Eretz Yisrael and challah in chutz la’aretz and then apply these principles to some practical situations.

### C. *Differences Between Challah of Eretz Yisrael and Chutz La’aretz*

We learned above that the majority of *posskim* maintain that the *mitzvah* of *hafrashas* *challah*, both in *Eretz Yisrael* and in *chutz la’aretz*, is currently rabbinic in nature. Nevertheless, there are a few situations in which the *posskim* are more *machmir* concerning *challah* in *Eretz Yisrael* than concerning *challah* in *chutz la’aretz.* The reason for this distinction is that the *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah* in *Eretz Yisrael* is fundamentally biblical in nature, and is only rabbinic today because the majority of Jews do not currently reside in Israel. In contrast, the rabbinic *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah* in *chutz la’aretz* was only enacted so that it would not be forgotten. We will list three practical distinctions between *challah* in *Eretz Yisrael* and *challah* in *chutz la’aretz* and then apply these principles to some practical situations. 

1) The S”A in **סימן שכג** (11) *passkins* that if *challah* separated in *chutz la’aretz* becomes mixed with permitted dough, the mixture is permitted even when the ratio is only 50-50. Furthermore, one may deliberately be *mevatel challah* of *chutz la’aretz.* The *Rama* argues on both points and *passkins* that if *challah* is mixed with other permissible dough, a ratio of 100:1 is required to permit the mixture. If it is mixed with a different type of food (i.e., מין בשאינו מינו), *shishim* is required. Furthermore, one is not allowed to intentionally be *mevatel* a rabbinic prohibition (see *Rama* סימן צט-ו). Thus, according to the S”A, *challah* in *chutz la’aretz* is treated far more leniently than *challah* in *Eretz Yisrael*.

2) We will learn below that *challah* should ideally be separated from the dough before it is baked. However, if one forgot, he may be *mafrish challah* after the bread is baked. The S”A (end of **סימן שכג-א**) *passkins,* based on the **גמרא ביצה** (ט.), that in *chutz la’aretz,* if one baked bread without being *mafrish challah,* he may eat the bread, provided he leaves over a small amount as *challah*. The *Rama* explains that one must leave enough bread so that after separating the *challah,* some bread still remains. In other words, the entire remaining piece may not be designated as *challah*; rather, a piece from it is removed as *challah.* In Eretz Yisrael, by contrast, there is no such provision of eating first and being *mafrish* later.

3) In *chutz la’aretz,* if the dough was divided into multiple loaves and only some are present, one may be *mafrish challah* from the loaves that are present and thereby exempt even the ones not physically present. In *Eretz Yisrael,* however, one should only be *mafrish challah* from bread that is physically present. This concept is known as הפרשה שלא מן המוקף. As we will learn below, if one is *mafrish* שלא מן המוקף in *Eretz Yisrael,* it is still valid after the fact. The *Rama* clarifies that even in *chutz la’aretz,* a *hafrasha* from one loaf of bread to another that is not present is valid only if they originated from the same batch of dough. If they were made from different batches, each of which is independently obligated in *hafrashas challah,* then even in *chutz la’aretz,* one may not be *mafrish* from one to the other if they are in separate locations.

blocks.text: Practical Applications:
Forgot to be mafrish challah for Shabbos challahs

What should you do if, on Shabbos night before the meal, your wife tells you that she forgot to be mafrish challah from the challahs[9] she baked? The S”A in או״ח סימן רסא-א (12) passkins that one is not allowed to be mafrish terumah on Shabbos, or even during bein ha’shmashos. The משנ״ב סק״ד explains that hafrashas challah is prohibited because of מתקן – making the remaining challah loaf permissible to eat is considered similar to fixing. Based on this, if you live in chutz la’aretz and remember that you were not mafrish challah during Shabbos, you may eat the challah and leave over a small amount that is large enough to be mafrish from after Shabbos. However, in Eretz Yisrael, you may not eat from the challah on Shabbos and you must wait until after Shabbos to be mafrish challah. Instead, you should borrow challah from a neighbor.

chunks.contentMarkdown:
<u>Eating some of the bread without being</u> *<u>mafrish</u>* 

What should you do if you began eating bread on a weekday and then remembered you had not yet been *mafrish challah*? In *chutz la’aretz,* the solution is simple – you may continue eating as long as you leave over a little bread and then be *mafrish challah* from the amount remaining. 

What should you do in *Eretz Yisrael,* where you are forbidden from taking another bite? The **חיד״א**, in ברכי יוסף (שכג-ד) (13), *passkins* that you should immediately be *mafrish challah* from the remaining bread and have in mind that the separation should also cover what you already ate. He explains that although the bread that was already eaten is no longer present, and it is generally forbidden to be *mafrish* in *Eretz Yisrael* on food that is not present, *be’dieved,* the *hafrashas challah* is valid, and one should do whatever is possible to rectify the situation. This principle, that a separation made on behalf of food that is not present is nevertheless valid *be’dieved*, is stated explicitly by the S”A in **סימן שלא-כה**. The S”A *paskins* that although one may not be *mafrish terumah* for produce that is not present, if one does so, the separation is valid. The ברכי יוסף extends this principle even to food that has already been consumed.

blocks.text: Gifting challah and forgetting to be mafrish

There once was a woman in Eretz Yisrael[11] who baked challah for Shabbos and sent it to her married children living in a different city. On Shabbos night, she remembered that she had forgotten to be mafrish challah and wanted to know if she can be mafrish on the remaining challah in her home and exempt those sent to her children. In this situation, there are two issues that need to be addressed. First, being mafrish on Shabbos is a rabbinic violation of מתקן (fixing), and second, in EY one may not be mafrish on bread that is not present. Nevertheless, we mentioned in the previous subsection that according to the חיד״א, in a be’dieved situation, being mafrish from one location to the other still works. The question is: may the mother violate these two rabbinic prohibitions of fixing and being mafrish on bread that is not present in order to prevent her children from sinning by eating the challah?

The **ברוך אומר** (יו״ד רכ) (14) quotes the **גמרא עירובין** (לב:), which teaches that a *chaver* (i.e., a *talmid chacham*) is allowed to be *mafrish* on food that is not before him, in order to prevent an *am ha’aretz* from eating *tevel* (food which *terumah* was not separated). The Gemara explains that although being *mafrish* on food that is not before him is forbidden, it is preferable for the *chaver* to violate the less severe prohibition of being *mafrish* on food that is not present, in order to prevent his friend from violating the more severe prohibition of eating *tevel*. 

**Tosfos,** in one[12] explanation, writes that this ruling applies only when it is the *chaver’s* fault that the individual will come to eat *tevel* (e.g., the *chaver* sent the *tevel* fruit without being *mafrish*). Based on this explanation of Tosfos, the ברוך אומר *passkins* that since it is the mother’s fault that her children will eat *tevel,* the mother is allowed to violate the lesser prohibition of being *mafrish* on food that is not before her and the lesser prohibition of being *mafrish* on Shabbos in order to prevent her children from transgressing the greater prohibition of eating *tevel*.

He concludes that since the mother is already being *mafrish* to save the loaves sent to her children, she should also include the remaining loaves she has at home (from which *challah* also was not taken off) in the same *hafrasha,* and she, too, would be allowed to eat them on Shabbos.

blocks.text: However, this approach would seem to be against the opinion of the נתיבות המשפט (רלד-ג) (15). Let’s explain. The נתיבות passkins that although one who unintentionally (b’shogeg) transgresses a biblical prohibition must do teshuva, one who unintentionally transgresses a rabbinic decree does not even need to do teshuva. The משנת יהושע (חושן מפשט-סז) (16) explains that regarding a biblical prohibition, the action itself is intrinsically forbidden (איסור חפצא), and even if one transgresses it unintentionally, he is required to do teshuva. For example, if one forgot it was Shabbos and lit a match, since the act is intrinsically forbidden, he is obligated to do teshuva, even if the violation was b’shogeg. In contrast, a rabbinic prohibition is understood as enacted upon the individual (גברא) to listen to Chazal, and when one inadvertently (b’shogeg) transgresses a rabbinic prohibition, it is not considered as if he did not listen to Chazal. Only intentionally disregarding Chazal is considered going against them, but accidentally not listening to them, is not considered “not listening” to them.

However, this approach would seem to be against the opinion of the **נתיבות המשפט** (רלד-ג) (15). Let’s explain. The נתיבות *passkins* that although one who unintentionally (*b’shogeg)* transgresses a biblical prohibition must do *teshuva,* one who unintentionally transgresses a rabbinic decree does not even need to do *teshuva.* The **משנת יהושע** (חושן מפשט-סז) (16) explains that regarding a biblical prohibition, the action itself is intrinsically forbidden (איסור חפצא), and even if one transgresses it unintentionally, he is required to do *teshuva*. For example, if one forgot it was Shabbos and lit a match, since the act is intrinsically forbidden, he is obligated to do *teshuva,* even if the violation was *b’shogeg.* In contrast, a rabbinic prohibition is understood as enacted upon the individual (גברא) to listen to *Chazal,* and when one inadvertently (*b’shogeg*) transgresses a rabbinic prohibition, it is not considered as if he did not listen to Chazal. Only intentionally disregarding Chazal is considered going against them, but accidentally not listening to them, is not considered “not listening” to them. 

Based on the reasoning of the נתיבות, even if the children unknowingly eat the *tevel* challah, they have done nothing wrong and would not be required to do *teshuva* because they **unintentionally** transgressed a **rabbinic** decree.[13] Therefore, the mother should be forbidden to violate the two prohibitions of being *mafrish* on Shabbos and from one location to other, because she is not saving them from a transgression that must be rectified. 

Nevertheless, there are several reasons why it still may be worthwhile for the mother to be *mafrish*: 1) Perhaps the majority of Jews in the world already live in *Eretz Yisrael* today, rendering the obligation of *hafrashas challah* a biblical one according to many opinions, as discussed above. 2)  It seems that the majority of *posskim* argue on the נתיבות, such as the **שער הציון** (שלד סקס״ה), who writes that one who unintentionally transgresses a rabbinic prohibition on Shabbos must do *teshuva. Le’maase,* one should ask their Rav regarding what to do on Shabbos, but during the week the majority of *posskim* are lenient and allow being *mafrish* on *challah* that is in a different location if there is no way to inform the recipient; see דרך אמונה (ציה״ל תרומות פ״ג-רפט). 

To summarize, if in EY you forgot to be *mafrish challah* before sending some of the bread elsewhere and only remembered on Shabbos: 

- The ברוך אומר allows transgressing the two lesser rabbinic prohibitions of being *mafrish* from one location onto another and being *mafrish* on Shabbos, in order to prevent others from transgressing the greater prohibition of eating *tevel.*

- The נתיבות would seemingly prohibit doing so, because the recipients in the other location do not transgress the rabbinic prohibition (since they did not know about it)*.*

- Some argue on the נתיבות, and some *passkin* that one is allowed to be *mafrish* in this case*.*

Source Notes

[13]:  In this case, where the children had no way of knowing that *challah* was not separated, there is even more reason to be lenient, since their mistake is more comparable to an *ones* than a *shogeg.*

chunks.title: Matzah — Why Hafrasha Is Often After Baking
chunks.summary: Matzah often has challah separated after baking due to chametz concerns and small batches; some consumers buy matzah to be mafrish themselves.
chunks.sectionTitle: Differences Between Challah of Eretz Yisrael and Chutz La’aretz

blocks.text: Forgetting to be mafrish challah from matzah

Ideally, the mitzvah of hafrashas challah should be performed right after the flour and water are mixed and made into dough (we will learn the precise ideal time below). However, with regard to matzah, the S”A in או״ח תנז passkins that the hafrashas challah should be performed after the matzah is baked, for two reasons. First, if the challah is separated from the batch of dough, the separated challah would have to be burned within eighteen minutes before it became chametz, and matzah bakeries do not want potential chametz in the facility during production. Second, the amount of flour used for each batch does not meet the required amount of flour needed for hafrashas challah.[14] Therefore, after the matzah is baked, they are placed all in a container or wagon and challah is separated from the entire container. Some matzah bakeries sell matzah from which challah has not yet been separated, allowing the consumer to recite the bracha and perform the mitzvah of hafrashas challah.

chunks.title: Forgot Matzah in Chu”l on Pesach Night
chunks.summary: Mishnah Berurah: leave over from each batch/piece as needed and separate after Yom Tov.

blocks.text: What should you do if you baked matzos as part of a group at a matzah bakery and forgot to be mafrish challah from your matzah afterward, and only realized on Pesach night? The משנ״ב (תנז סק״י) (17) writes that being mafrish on Yom Tov is forbidden just as it is on Shabbos. Therefore, if the obligation to be mafrish already took effect before Yom Tov (e.g., the matzos were combined in a container, or there was enough dough in each batch separately), then the משנ"ב writes that in chu”l, the halacha is as follows. If you know which matzos came from each batch (e.g., you bought a batch of whole wheat and a batch of regular flour and can differentiate between them), you should leave over a matzah from each batch and then be mafrish from it after Yom Tov. If you do not know which matzah came from which batch (e.g., you bought two batches of regular flour matzah and each batch was obligated in challah), you must leave over a small piece from every single matzah. After Yom Tov, you combine all of those pieces into a container and be mafrish from there. In the שער הציון (כא), the Chafetz Chaim explains that since all the leftover pieces were combined into a container, one hafrasha suffices for all of them.

The above guidelines apply only in *chutz la’aretz,* where you may leave over some of the *matzah* and be *mafrish* after Yom Tov. What should you do if you are in *Eretz Yisrael*? There are three possible solutions.

	1) The **שמירת שבת כהלכתה** (פרק יא-טז) (18), citing **Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach**, *passkins* that in *Eretz Yisrael,* if there is no other way to get kosher *matzah* (e.g., a Pesach program that only brought *matzah* from which *challah* was not separated)*,* one is allowed to be *mafrish* on Pesach in order to fulfill the biblical *mitzvah* of eating *matzah.* Similarly, on the first night of Sukkos, when there is a biblical obligation to eat a כזית of bread in the *sukkah,* if you forgot to be *mafrish* and there is no other way to obtain bread, you are allowed to be *mafrish*. He adds that when being *mafrish* in *Eretz Yisrael* on Yom Tov, it is best to make the declaration mentally without verbalizing it and without reciting a *bracha* (but the physical separation still needs to be performed)*.* In the footnote (נח), he explains that the above only works in Eretz Yisrael, but in *chutz la’aretz,* one should leave over from each *matzah* or bread. 

	2) The חלת לחם (סימן י-ז) suggests another alternative, but to properly understand it, we first need to learn two important *halachos.*

1. The **באור הלכה** (סימן שמג) (19), quoting the רשב״א (as understood by the ר״ן), *passkins* that a child is allowed to violate an *issur* *derabanan* if it is for his own sake. Therefore, if you forget to bring a *siddur* to *shul* and there is no *eiruv,* the *katan* is allowed to bring one for himself, and you may follow along with him. (The שש״כ (יח-סא) *passkins* in accordance with this באור הלכה.)

2. The **רמב״ם** (תרומות פ״ד-ה) *passkins* that if a *katan* who has reached the age at which his or her oaths are binding, and he/she separates *terumah,* the *terumah* is valid. The S”A in **יו״ד סימן רלג** *passkins* that the vows of a 12-year-old boy or 11-year-old girl who understand to Whom they are making a vow are valid. Accordingly, the S”A in **סימן שלא-לג** *passkins* that the *terumah* taken by such a *katan* is binding.[15]

Based on these two *halachos*, the **חלת לחם** (סימן י-ז) (20) suggests that it is best to give the *matzah* as a gift to the child (a 12-year-old boy or 11-year-old girl) and have them be *mafrish* it for themselves. Since their *hafrasha* is valid, everyone else can benefit from the *matzah* as well*.*

	3) **RSZA**, in הליכות שלמה (פ״ט-א) (21), suggests that immediately before Pesach begins, the Rav of the community should be *mafrish challah* while having in mind all of those who forgot to do so in his community. In fact, Rav Boyer of Bnei Brak is *mafrish challah* every *erev-*Shabbos 40 minutes before *shekiyah* on behalf of Jews all over the world.[16] This *hafrasha* is effective because it is a *zechus* for those who forgot, and one may act on another person’s behalf when doing so is entirely for that person’s benefit (i.e., the rule of זכין לאדם שלא בפניו). Indeed, RSZA himself used to do this in *Shaarei Chessed.*[17] In the footnote, he explains that the reason it must be done shortly before Yom Tov begins is that if the Rav is *mafrish* earlier in the day and a member of the community is *mafrish* later in the day, the Rav’s *hafrasha* is no longer a *zechus* for this individual, because he prefers to be *yotze* and recite the *bracha* himself*.* Furthermore, the **חקת הפסח** (פכ״ו-סק״יג) goes so far as to claim that if the Rav performs the *hafrasha* in the morning, he could be causing those who are *mafrish* later in the day to recite a *bracha le’vatallah.* 

However, there is a significant difficulty with RSZA’s suggestion: We learned above that it is forbidden to be *mafrish* from one location to another in *Eretz Yisrael,* and even in *chu”l,* one may not separate from one batch of dough for another. How, then, was he able to be *mafrish* for others? 

The **מנחת יצחק** (ח״ד-נט) (22) explains that this may still be permitted because *bedieved, challah* may be separated even from one batch for another based on what we learned above that a *chaver* is allowed to transgress a lesser prohibition to save another from transgressing a more severe one. Although we learned that Tosfos only allows if the *chaver* is the one who caused the other to violate the prohibition (and here the Rav of the community is not responsible for others forgetting to be *mafrish*), there are two possible solutions for why it is permitted. First, Tosfos in his second answer writes that a *chaver* is allowed to transgress the lesser prohibition even if he is not responsible for his friend consuming *tevel,* and this is how we *passkin lema’ase,* as the **משנ״ב** סימן שו-סקנ״ו writes. Second, even according to Tosfos’ first answer, Tosfos agrees that a *chaver* may still transgress a lesser prohibition on behalf of the public even if he is not responsible for it. Thus, RSZA felt that it is better to transgress the lesser prohibition of being *mafrish* from one location to the other in order to allow people who forgot to be *mafrish* to be able to eat their *matzah.* This is also the *pssak* of **משפטי ארץ** (פ״ה-כא).

blocks.text: Sending matzah to chutz la’aretz

We learned above that if one forgot to be mafrish challah in chutz la’aretz, he may leave over some of the bread/matzah used on Shabbos or Yom Tov[18] and then be mafrish from what is left, but in Eretz Yisrael, it is forbidden. The רמב״ם (ביכורים פ״ה-ו) passkins, as explained by the כסף משנה and משנה למלך, that the biblical obligation of hafrashas challah applies only to flour that is made into dough in Eretz Yisrael, regardless of where the wheat is from.[19] Conversely, flour made from wheat of Eretz Yisrael which is brought to chutz la’aretz and made into dough there is only rabbinically obligated in challah, similar to all challah in chu”l. Many times, matzah bakeries ship their matzah from Israel to chu”l and vice versa. In light of the רמב"ם, what should be done if you baked matzah with a group of people in a bakery and forgot to be mafrish challah?

chunks.contentMarkdown:
<u>Sending</u> *<u>matzah</u>* <u>to</u> *<u>chutz la’aretz</u>*

	We learned above that if one forgot to be *mafrish challah* in *chutz la’aretz,* he may leave over some of the bread/*matzah* used on Shabbos or Yom Tov[18] and then be *mafrish* from what is left, but in *Eretz Yisrael,* it is forbidden. The **רמב״ם** (ביכורים פ״ה-ו) *passkins,* as explained by the כסף משנה and משנה למלך, that the **biblical** obligation of *hafrashas challah* applies only to flour that is made into dough in *Eretz Yisrael,* regardless of where the wheat is from.[19] Conversely, flour made from wheat of *Eretz Yisrael* which is brought to *chutz la’aretz* and made into dough there is only **rabbinically** obligated in *challah,* similar to all *challah* in *chu”l.* Many times, *matzah* bakeries ship their *matzah* from Israel to *chu”l* and vice versa. In light of the רמב"ם, what should be done if you baked *matzah* with a group of people in a bakery and forgot to be *mafrish challah*?	

	If the *challah* was made in *chu”l* and sent to EY*,* one should leave over from every single *matzah* and then, on *Chol Ha’moed,* place them all in a container and be *mafrish* from the container, as mentioned above in the משנ״ב. However, if the *matzah* was made in *EY*, it would seem that one is not allowed to eat any of it before being *mafrish,* even if the *matzah* is now located in *chu”l,* and one should do what was suggested in the previous subsection. Nevertheless, the **חשב האפוד** (ח״ב-מג) (23), quoting the ב״ח, understands the רמב״ם differently and *passkins* that *challah* that was taken from *EY* to *chu”l* is only rabbinically obligated in *challah.* Therefore, you should eat the *matzah* and leave over a small portion from each piece to be *mafrish* from afterward. However, the **משפטי ארץ** (פ״ט-א) *passkins* like the כסף משנה and משנה למלך’s understanding of the רמב״ם above, and one would not be allowed to be *mafrish.* 

Source Notes

[18]:  It should be noted that the S”A in סימן תקו-ג *passkins* that if the batch of dough was made on Yom Tov, you are allowed to be *mafrish.* It is forbidden to be *mafrish* on YT only if the dough was made before YT.

[19]:  As of today, most flour in *Eretz Yisrael* comes from *chutz la’aretz.*

blocks.text: Bracha when mafrish after eating

We learned above that if one forgot to be mafrish challah before Shabbos or YT in chu”l, he may eat and leave over some bread from which to be mafrish from after Shabbos or YT. RSZA, quoted in שש״כ (פמ״ב-הע׳ נז), passkins that one should not recite a bracha when being mafrish after Shabbos. Since the bread was intentionally set aside on Shabbos for the hafrasha after Shabbos, it is viewed as having taken effect retroactively on Shabbos. Therefore, one cannot recite a bracha on Motzaei Shabbos for a hafrasha that is deemed to have already occurred. However, the ערה״ש (או״ח שכג-ג) and Rav Chaim Kanievsky דרך אמונה, ביכורים פ״ה- סקקכא)) passkin that one should recite a bracha when being mafrish since the Gemara does not say otherwise.

chunks.contentMarkdown:
*D.   How Much to be Mafrish?*

After learning the basic differences between *hafrashas challah* in EY and *chu”l,* in this section we will discuss how much dough to be *mafrish*. We will learn that initially, in *Eretz Yisrael,* one baking bread at home needed to be *mafrish* 1/24 of the dough, while a baker was required to be *mafrish* only 1/48 of the batch. Today, however, the amount separated has changed, as will be explained below.

chunks.title: Rambam: One Mitzvah, Any Amount Biblically
chunks.summary: Rambam: separating and giving are one mitzvah; any amount works biblically, 1/24 or 1/48 is respectable amount.

blocks.text: In order to understand why 1/24 and 1/48 were originally the required amounts for hafrasha, we first need to better understand the structure and framework of the mitzvah of hafrashas challah. The רמב״ם (עשה-קלג) (24) passkins that there is one mitzvah of separating challah from the dough and giving it to the kohen. In הלכות ביכורים (פ״ה-א), the רמב״ם explains that, biblically speaking, one may fulfill the mitzvah by separating and giving even the smallest amount. However, the verse ״תתן לו״ – “you shall give him,” teaches that you should separate an amount that is worthy of giving, which is 1/24 of a household’s batch of dough and 1/48 from a baker’s batch.

The רמב״ם in פירוש המשניות explains further that when baking at home, a larger portion of 1/24 is needed in order to fulfill the passuk of “giving,” which implies a respectable amount. A baker, in contrast, who prepares much larger batches of dough, gives a smaller percentage of 1/48, which generally results in the same amount of dough as 1/24 of a household batch. The Mishnah adds that if the batch of dough becomes tamei, only 1/48 is separated.

chunks.contentMarkdown:
In order to understand why 1/24 and 1/48 were originally the required amounts for *hafrasha,* we first need to better understand the structure and framework of the *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah.* The **רמב״ם** (עשה-קלג) (24) *passkins* that there is one *mitzvah* of separating *challah* from the dough and giving it to the *kohen.* In הלכות ביכורים (פ״ה-א), the **רמב״ם** explains that, biblically speaking, one may fulfill the *mitzvah* by separating and giving even the smallest amount. However, the verse ״תתן לו״ – “you shall give him,” teaches that you should separate an amount that is worthy of giving, which is 1/24 of a household’s batch of dough and 1/48 from a baker’s batch. 

These amounts of 1/24 and 1/48 originate in the **משנה חלה** (פ״ב-ז) (25), which teaches that one who bakes bread at home must separate 1/24 of the dough, even if baking for a large number of guests, while a baker need separate only 1/48 of the dough. The **רמב״ם** in פירוש המשניות explains further that when baking at home, a larger portion of 1/24 is needed in order to fulfill the *passuk* of “giving,” which implies a respectable amount. A baker, in contrast, who prepares much larger batches of dough, gives a smaller percentage of 1/48, which generally results in the same amount of dough as 1/24 of a household batch. The Mishnah adds that if the batch of dough becomes *tamei,* only 1/48 is separated.

It seems clear from the רמב״ם that since separating and giving constitute one *mitzvah,* and biblically one fulfills the obligation with any amount, his writing that one must give 1/24 or 1/48 to fulfill the *passuk* of “giving a respectable amount” must be only an אסמכתא. Indeed, the **מזרחי** on Rashi (במדבר פט״ו-כא) writes explicitly that the verse is only an אסמכתא.

blocks.text: The רמב״ן (השגות-שורש יב) (26) argues on the רמב״ם and passkins that hafrashas challah consists of two distinct mitzvos: 1) Separating dough as challah, thereby rendering the remaining dough permissible to eat (and no longer tevel). 2) Giving the dough to the kohen.

blocks.text: The נודע ביהודה (יו״ד תנינא -רא) (27) writes that even giving 1/24 or 1/48 can constitute part of the biblical obligation. He explains that since there are two parts to the mitzvah of hafrashas challah, separating and giving, whenever one separates even the smallest amount, he biblically fulfills the mitzvah of separating. However, when giving the dough to a kohen, the נודע ביהודה suggests that the biblical amount one must separate is always 1/24 of the minimum quantity of flour required for hafrashas challah (one-tenth of an eifah, which we will learn below is between 1.2-2.2 kg). If one prepares only the minimum amount of dough that requires hafrashas challah, then there is a biblical commandment to give an amount that is considered a meaningful gift, i.e., 1/24 of a household batch and 1/48 of a baker’s batch (which is roughly the same amount since the baker bakes more). However, if a household batch is prepared to be double the biblical amount required to be mafrish, on a biblical level, he needs to give 1/48 of the batch of dough, while rabbinically, he needs to give 1/24 of the actual batch.[20]

chunks.contentMarkdown:
The **רמב״ן** (השגות-שורש יב) (26) argues on the רמב״ם and *passkins* that *hafrashas challah* consists of two distinct *mitzvos*: 1) Separating dough as *challah*, thereby rendering the remaining dough permissible to eat (and no longer *tevel*). 2) Giving the dough to the *kohen.*

The **נודע ביהודה** (יו״ד תנינא -רא) (27) writes that even giving 1/24 or 1/48 can constitute part of the biblical obligation. He explains that since there are two parts to the *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah,* separating and giving, whenever one separates even the smallest amount, he biblically fulfills the *mitzvah* of separating. However, when giving the dough to a *kohen,* the נודע ביהודה suggests that the biblical amount one must separate is always 1/24 of the minimum quantity of flour required for *hafrashas challah* (one-tenth of an *eifah,* which we will learn below is between 1.2-2.2 kg). If one prepares only the minimum amount of dough that requires *hafrashas challah*, then there is a biblical commandment to give an amount that is considered a meaningful gift, i.e., 1/24 of a household batch and 1/48 of a baker’s batch (which is roughly the same amount since the baker bakes more). However, if a household batch is prepared to be double the biblical amount required to be *mafrish*, on a biblical level, he needs to give 1/48 of the batch of dough, while rabbinically, he needs to give 1/24 of the actual batch.[20] 

To summarize:

- The רמב״ם *passkins* that separating and giving *challah* constitute one *mitzvah* that can be fulfilled with any amount, but rabbinically, one should give 1/24 of a household batch of dough and 1/48 of a baker’s batch since that is defined as a respectable portion.

- The רמב״ן argues that there are two *mitzvos* – separating and giving.

- According to theנודע ביהודה, the biblical *mitzvah* of separating is fulfilled by separating any amount, while the biblical *mitzvah* of giving is fulfilled by giving 1/24 from the minimum quantity of dough required for *hafrashas challah.* (If the batch is larger than the minimum quantity, 1/24 is still given, but any amount above 1/24 of the minimum quantity is rabbinic.)

Source Notes

[20]:  Most understand that the נודע ביהודה only makes sense within the רמב״ן who learns that there are two parts to the *mitzvah,* but the שבט הלוי (ח״ב-קעח סק״ב) understands that the נודע ביהודה can even fit within the רמב״ם.

blocks.text: How do we passkin? The S”A in סימן שכב-א (28) quotes the language of the רמב״ם that there is a biblical mitzvah to separate challah and give it to a kohen, and the biblical requirement is fulfilled by separating even the smallest amount. However, on a rabbinic level, one should give 1/24 of a household batch of dough and 1/48 of a baker’s batch. The S”A adds, based on the משנה חלה (פ״ב-ז) quoted above, that if the challah becomes tamei and will be burned anyway, even a private individual at home  need separate only 1/48.

blocks.text: All of the above pertains to hafrashas challah in EY, but in chu”l, the halacha is somewhat different, as we will see. The משנה חלה (פ״ד-ח) states that the world is divided into three regions: Parts of EY that were sanctified by Ezra, parts of EY that were not sanctified by Ezra, and the rest of the world. The Mishna explains that the number of challos (i.e., pieces of dough, one or two) separated and the size of each challah varies by region. In parts of EY that were sanctified by Ezra only one challah is separated, and in the other parts of EY that were not sanctified by Ezra and in chu”l, two challahs are separated, one that is burned and another that is given to a kohen.[21]

blocks.text: How do we passkin lema’ase? Ashkenazim passkin like the Rama that any amount of challah may be separated, although the custom is to take a kezayis, and it should be burned. Regarding Sephardim, the בית יוסף writes that the minhag is to be mafrish only one challah and burn it, and it seems the בית יוסף is referring to both EY and chu”l (like the Rama). chunks.contentMarkdown:
How do we *passkin*? The S”A in **סימן שכב-א** (28) quotes the language of the רמב״ם that there is a biblical *mitzvah* to separate *challah* and give it to a *kohen*, and the biblical requirement is fulfilled by separating even the smallest amount. However, on a rabbinic level, one should give 1/24 of a household batch of dough and 1/48 of a baker’s batch. The S”A adds, based on the **משנה חלה** (פ״ב-ז) quoted above, that if the *challah* becomes *tamei* and will be burned anyway, even a private individual at home  need separate only 1/48. 

All of the above pertains to *hafrashas challah* in *EY,* but in *chu”l,* the *halacha* is somewhat different, as we will see*.* The **משנה חלה** (פ״ד-ח) states that the world is divided into three regions: Parts of *EY* that were sanctified by Ezra, parts of *EY* that were not sanctified by Ezra, and the rest of the world. The Mishna explains that the number of *challos* (i.e., pieces of dough, one or two) separated and the size of each *challah* varies by region. In parts of *EY* that were sanctified by Ezra only one *challah* is separated, and in the other parts of *EY* that were not sanctified by Ezra and in *chu”l,* two *challahs* are separated, one that is burned and another that is given to a *kohen*.[21] 

There is a three-way dispute among the *Rishonim* regarding how to understand this *Mishnah.* For the sake of clarity and brevity, we will only discuss the rulings of the S”A, *Rama*, and the practical *halacha* today, which is agreed upon by both *Ashkenazim* and *Sephardim*. 

In EY, everyone agrees that one *challah* is separated and burned. In *chu”l,* the **S”A** in סעיפים ד-ה (29) *passkins* that you may either separate two, one which is burned and the other which is given to any *kohen,* or you may separate one (the size of 1/48 of the dough)[22] and give it to a *kohen* who is not *tamei* with *tumah* that emanates from his body (i.e., *baal keri, niddah, zav,* or *zava*). The ***Rama*** in סעיף ה argues that both in *EY* and in *chu”l,* only one *challah* is separated. It may be of any size, although the custom is to separate a *kezayis*, and it should be burned*.* 

The **ט״ז** (ה) explains that the custom is to burn the *challah* rather than give it to any *kohen* since we are not certain who is definitely a *kohen* today. The *Rama* adds that if a *kohen* does eat the *challah,* he should first recite a special *bracha.*[23]

To summarize:

- In <u>EY</u> one *challah* is separated and burned.

  - **S”A** – *challah* should be the size of 1/48 of the dough.

  - ***Rama*** – any amount, although the custom is a *kezayis.*

- In *<u>chu”l</u>*:

  - **S”A** – either separate two *challos*, burn one and give the other to a *kohen,* even if he is *tamei,* or separate one *challah* and give it to a *kohen* who is not *tamei* with a *tumah* that  emanates from his body.

  - ***Rama*** – today, both in EY and in *chu”l,* only one *challah* of any size is separated, but preferably should be the size of a *kezayis,* and it is burned (because we are not certain who is a real *kohen*).

How do we *passkin lema’ase*? *Ashkenazim passkin* like the *Rama* that any amount of *challah* may be separated, although the custom is to take a *kezayis,* and it should be burned*.* Regarding *Sephardim,* the **בית יוסף** writes that the *minhag* is to be *mafrish* only one challah and burn it, and it seems the בית יוסף is referring to both EY and *chu”l* (like the *Rama*)*.* The **ברכי יוסף** (שכב-ב) (30) writes that although the S”A does not quote it here, in **סימן שלא-יט** he *passkins* that since *terumah* today is burned, it suffices to separate any amount, and the same would apply to *challah.* **Rav Ovadya** in הליכות עולם (ח״ג-עמ׳ מט) also *passkins* that even *Sephardim* should only separate one *challah,* which may be any size, and it should be burned. 

Source Notes

[21]:  The ירושלמי (חלה פ״ד-ד) explains the reason for why areas of *EY* not sanctified by Ezra require two *challahs* to be separated. The first *challah* is separated and burned because *Chazal* decreed a *tumah* status on *chu”l* as well as areas of *EY* not sanctified by Ezra (טומאת ארץ העמים). However, since many are not aware of this *tumah* status, they might be led to believe that all separated *challah* needs to be burned. For this reason, we give a second *challah* to the *kohen.* But we also cannot give the *kohen* one *challah* alone because then those who are aware of the *tumah* status will think that *challah* which is *tamei* may be eaten. For this reason, both *challahs* are necessary. In regular *chu”l,* the רמב״ם (ביכורים פ״ה-ח) explains that the first *challah* is burned because *chu”l* is *tamei,* and the second is given to the *kohen* so we do not forget about *challah.* 

[22]:  The smallest amount size is used since the *hafrasha* is in *chu”l.*

[23]:  The *Rama* in *hilchos* Pesach in סימן תנז writes that a *kohen* child may eat *matzah* made from the *hafrashas challah* dough*.* The **ש״ך** (שכב-ט) asks that the *Rama* seems to be contradicting himself. Here he *passkins* that the custom is to burn *challah,* yet in *Hilchos* Pesach he *passkins* that one may give it to a *katan?* The ש״ך answers that one must differentiate between Pesach and other times of the year. The **מג״א** (תנז-ט) explains that on *Erev Pesach* (and Pesach) the custom is to give the *challah* to a child *kohen* since there are a lot of *challahs* being separated and if they don’t eat from the *challah*, people might question whether they are *kohanim*. The **ערה״ש** (שכב-כא) proves that the *Rama* agrees to this distinction that there are times when *kohanim* do eat the *challah,* since here he writes the *nussach* of the *bracha* a *kohen* would recite when eating the *challah.*

chunks.contentMarkdown:
### E. *What To Do with the Separated Challah?*

After learning that today both *Sephardim* and *Ashkenazim* agree that approximately a *kezayis* of *challah* should be separated and burned, we will now delve into the *halachos* of burning the *challah.* 

The **גמרא שבת** (כה.) (31) teaches that just like there is a *mitzvah* to burn *kodshim* (e.g., *korbanos*) that became *tamei,* so too, there is a *mitzvah* to burn *terumah* (and *challah*) that have become *tamei.* The Gemara adds that when the *terumah/challah* is being burned, the *kohen* is allowed to benefit from the fire, but a *Yisrael* may not*.* **Rashi** explains that *terumah* is burned either because it is similar to *kodshim*, or because leaving it unburned might lead one to accidentally benefit from it. Most *Rishonim*[24] understand that there is an obligation to specifically burn *tamei terumah* and *challah,* rather than merely disposing of them.

The S”A in **סעיף ד** and the *Rama* in **סעיף ה** (29) *passkin* that the *challah* should be burned in a separate fire because a non-*kohen* may not benefit from its burning. The *Rama* adds that the custom in his time was to burn the *challah* before using the oven, because if food is baked in the oven while the *challah* is being burned, one benefits from the additional flames and heat created by the burning of the *challah.* The **חלקת בנימין** (שכב סקצ״ז) (32) explains that although placing the *challah* in the oven after it is fully heated will also increase the temperature (and thus cause benefit to be derived from the *challah*), that increase is so minimal that it is not considered benefiting from the *challah.* 

Source Notes

[24]:  See Tosfos there ד״ה כך and אגרות משה (יו״ד ח״ג-קכט).

chunks.title: Burning Challah Today in an Oven
chunks.summary: In modern ovens, burning may not add meaningful heat, but should be double-wrapped to avoid reicha/zeiah concerns.
chunks.sectionTitle: What To Do with the Separated Challah?

blocks.text: Practical Applications
Burning challah today

What is the best way to burn challah today? Are you required to burn the challah before baking the bread? The חלקת בנימין (שכב סקצ״ט) (32) passkins that since our gas ovens are already fully heated when baking, the burning challah inside does not increase the temperature in the oven. Therefore, baking other food while the challah is being burned is not considered benefiting from the burning of the challah. Nevertheless, since the challah is forbidden to be eaten (and the prohibition is more severe than eating pork[25]), you should make sure to double wrap the challah in aluminum foil to avoid any issues of ריחא or זיעא that could forbid the other food in the oven or the oven itself.

chunks.title: Ripped Tinfoil in Oven
chunks.summary: Reviews reicha/zeiah; Rav Moshe/Chayei Halevi permit other food if challah exposed, but rack needs libun; some argue even bread emits steam.
chunks.sectionTitle: What To Do with the Separated Challah?

blocks.text: Ripped tinfoil

What is the halacha if you are burning challah in an oven with other food and forgot to cover the challah or if the aluminum foil ripped as the challah expanded during baking? Is the other food permitted? To answer this question, we will briefly review what we learned in the halachos of basar b’chalav. Whenever two foods are cooked in an oven, where one food is forbidden and the other is permitted, or one is meat and the other dairy, there are two issues that need to be considered: 1) ריחא – the transfer of smell/aroma from one food to the other, and 2) זיעה – the transfer of steam.

Whenever two foods are cooked in an oven, where one food is forbidden and the other is permitted, or one is meat and the other dairy, there are two issues that need to be considered: 1) ריחא – the transfer of smell/aroma from one food to the other, and 2) זיעה – the transfer of steam.

blocks.text: The S”A in קח-א passkins that be’dieved, we do not take ריחא into consideration. Therefore, if you cooked dry meat with dry cheese in the same oven simultaneously (such that there is no issue of זיעה), both are permitted, even though the smell/aroma mix. However, if the meat or cheese were moist (and many posskim assume that most foods are moist), there is an issue of זיעה, because the steam from one food enters the other. Many posskim hold that even using the same oven for dairy and then meat (or vice versa) is forbidden because the steam from the dairy food is absorbed into the walls of the oven and is later released when you cook meat.

chunks.title: Throwing Out Challah When Burning Is Not Possible
chunks.summary: Ideally burn; Rav Ovadya and others allow less than kezayis wrapped/disposed when no way to burn.
chunks.sectionTitle: What To Do with the Separated Challah?

blocks.text: Disposing of Challah

Based on the גמרא שבת (31) and the pssak of the S”A and Rama, it seems clear that separated challah should be burned. Some, however, wrap the challah and throw it out, basing their practice on Rashi in the above Gemara and the חזון איש (סוף קונטרס תרו"מ ודמאי טו-א), who writes that one can dispose of teruma in this manner, and the same would presumably apply to challah. However, the מנחת יצחק (ח״ד-יג) argues that the חזון איש was lenient only with regard to terumah, but not with challah (see there for his reasoning). Thus, it would seem that the challah should always be burned.

chunks.title: Must Challah Be Burned Immediately?
chunks.summary: Some require immediate burning; others allow saving/freezing in a marked bag; best to burn soon.
chunks.sectionTitle: What To Do with the Separated Challah?

blocks.text: Disposing of challah right away

Are you obligated to burn the challah immediately, or may you hold on to it and burn it at a later time? The חלה כהלכתה (סימן א-יב שיח הארץ) (36) passkins that the challah must be burned immediately in order to avoid the possibility of accidentally benefiting from it. He explains that although the Rama, ש״ך and ט״ז permit leaving terumah in one’s possession before burning it, challah is much more common, and one must burn it immediately.

chunks.title: Fork Used in Burning Challah
chunks.summary: Fork inserted into unburned challah becomes treif and likely needs libun; use tongs on wrapped challah.
chunks.sectionTitle: What To Do with the Separated Challah?

blocks.text: Fork

The אמרי יעקב (ארץ ישראל סימן ב, ילקוטים סקמ״ג) (38) writes that when burning challah in the oven, you should make sure not to stick a fork into it to determine if it is fully burned because if it is not, the fork would absorb forbidden flavor from the challah and become treif. He writes that if the fork does become treif from inserting into the challah, since it absorbed through dry heat inside an oven, hagallah would not suffice, and one would need to perform libun on the fork. The best way to remove the wrapped challah is with a set of tongs. Since the challah is double wrapped, you may even use your regular tongs, as flavor does not travel through the two layers of foil (as we learned in a previous SCP zman and will be discussed below regarding two pots touching one another).

chunks.title: Burning Challah on Stovetop
chunks.summary: Better to place challah on foil; issue whether grates absorb and need libun; Rav Moshe likely lenient when wrapped.
chunks.sectionTitle: What To Do with the Separated Challah?

blocks.text: Burning on the stove top

Some have the custom to burn the challah on the stovetop. Although, in theory, one may burn the challah directly on the grates, it is best to place the challah on a piece of aluminum foil for two reasons: 1) It prevents the grates from getting dirty, and 2) the קובץ מבית לוי passkins that the grates  become non-kosher. Let’s explain.

blocks.text: The קובץ מבית לוי (ח״א עמ׳ כט) (39) quotes the משנ״ב in Hilchos Pesach, who passkins that for Pesach, grates do not require libun for two reasons: 1) Even if the grates have absorbed chametz, the chametz flavor cannot transfer to the pot sitting on the grates. The reason is that it is similar to two pots touching one another (on the outside), where the flavor does not travel from one to the other unless there is moisture in between them (or in between the grates and the pot). 2) Any chametz flavor absorbed in the grates is immediately burned out by the flames below. The קובץ מבית לוי explains that the second reason of the משנ״ב only applied in the time of the משנ״ב where the grates were directly on the fire, but stovetop grates today are elevated above the fire. Consequently, even if the flames come in contact with the grates, that is only a small part of the grates. Therefore, the קובץ מבית לוי rules that on Erev Pesach one should be sure to perform libun on his grates. Similarly, regarding challah, one should be careful not to burn the challah directly on the grates.[27] Rav Elyashiv in אשרי האיש (יו״ד ח״ב עמ׳ קסה) also passkins that one should not burn his challah on the grates.

chunks.contentMarkdown:
<u>Burning on the stove top</u>

	Some have the custom to burn the *challah* on the stovetop. Although, in theory, one may burn the *challah* directly on the grates, it is best to place the *challah* on a piece of aluminum foil for two reasons: 1) It prevents the grates from getting dirty, and 2) the קובץ מבית לוי *passkins* that the grates  become non-kosher. Let’s explain.

The **קובץ מבית לוי** (ח״א עמ׳ כט) (39) quotes the משנ״ב in *Hilchos Pesach,* who *passkins* that for Pesach, grates do not require *libun* for two reasons: 1) Even if the grates have absorbed *chametz,* the *chametz* flavor cannot transfer to the pot sitting on the grates. The reason is that it is similar to two pots touching one another (on the outside), where the flavor does not travel from one to the other unless there is moisture in between them (or in between the grates and the pot). 2) Any *chametz* flavor absorbed in the grates is immediately burned out by the flames below. The קובץ מבית לוי explains that the second reason of the משנ״ב only applied in the time of the משנ״ב where the grates were directly on the fire, but stovetop grates today are elevated above the fire. Consequently, even if the flames come in contact with the grates, that is only a small part of the grates. Therefore, the קובץ מבית לוי rules that on *Erev* Pesach one should be sure to perform *libun* on his grates. Similarly, regarding *challah,* one should be careful not to burn the *challah* directly on the grates.[27] Rav Elyashiv in אשרי האיש (יו״ד ח״ב עמ׳ קסה) also *passkins* that one should not burn his *challah* on the grates. 

**Rav Moshe** in אגרו״מ יו״ד (ח״א-קכד) *passkins* that you do not need separate grates for meat and dairy. Presumably, he would hold that if you wrap the *challah* with foil, you can burn it directly on the grates, just like any other meat and dairy pot that is placed directly on the grates.

Source Notes

[27]:  Based on this, he is also *machmir* to have separate grates for meat and dairy.

chunks.contentMarkdown:
### F. *Amount of Dough Needed to be Mafrish*

After learning how much *challah* should be separated from the dough (a *kezayis*)[28] and that it is best to burn the *challah,* in this section we will discuss the minimum amount of dough needed to create the obligation of *hafrashas challah.* While discussing this question*,* we will also encounter one of the most important *halachic* issues that arises on a daily basis: the calculation of the size of a *kezayis* and *beitzah.* As usual, we will begin with the earliest sources and work our way down to the modern-day *posskim.* After doing so, we will be able to better understand why the calculations of a *kezayis* and *beitzah* vary so greatly among the *posskim.* 

This extremely important and eye-opening *limud* will also impact on many other *halachos* that relate to the size of a *kezayis*, *beitzah*, or *revi’is,* such as the amount required to *bentch* or recite a *bracha acharona*, the size of *matzah* and *maror* eaten on *Pesach*, the minimum volume needed for your *kiddush* cup, and much more. By the end of this section, you will finally understand why the *shiurim* of the חזון איש are almost double the *shiurim* of other *posskim,* and why the opinions regarding the amount of flour needed for *hafrashas challah* vary so greatly*.* Let’s begin! 

We will begin by learning which types of flour are obligated in *hafrashas challah*, followed by the minimum amount of flour required. We will then explore how to calculate that amount, examine an apparent contradiction within that calculation, and finally see the reconciliation that forever changed the understanding of *shiurim*.

Source Notes

[28]:  Unless you do not burn the *challah,* in which case we learned that it is best to separate less than a *kezayis.*

chunks.title: Five Grains and One-Tenth of an Eifah
chunks.summary: Only five grains are obligated; minimum amount is an omer, one-tenth of an eifah.
chunks.sectionTitle: Amount of Dough Needed to be Mafrish

blocks.text: I. The type and amount

The משנה חלה (פ״א-א) (40) teaches that only dough made from the five species of grain is obligated in challah. The five grains are: Wheat (חיטה), barley (שעורה), spelt (כוסמין), oats (שיבולת שועל),[29] and rye (שיפון).  The Bartenura explains that the mitzvah of hafrashas challah is linked to Pesach because both use the word ״לחם״. Just like matzah may only be made from the five grains that can rise and become chametz, so too, the mitzvah of hafrashas challah only applies to dough made from the five grains.

Now that we know which types of flour require *hafrasha*, we can learn about the minimum amount needed. The **גמרא עירובין** (פג:) (41) derives from a *passuk* that the obligation to be *mafrish challah* applies only from a batch of dough equal in size to the portion of manna (*man*) in the *midbar* – an *omer,* which is 1/10 of an *eifah.*

chunks.contentMarkdown:
<u>II. The calculation</u>

How much is 1/10 of an *eifah*? There is an important acronym that every learned Jew should know that will help you determine **any** measurement you ever encounter when learning Mishnah, Gemara, or *halacha.* The acronym is **כאסקלב יגודו**— where **כאסקלב**  represents the units of measurement: **כ**ור, **א**יפה, **ס**אה, **ק**ב, **ל**וג, **ב**יצה. The word **יגודו** provides the numerical relationship between each unit, indicating how many of each measure is contained within the next. Thus, a כור contains 10 איפה, an איפה contains 3 סאה, a סאה contains 6 קב, a קב contains 4 לוגין, and a לוג contains 6 ביצים. See below. 

![Hebrew measurement mnemonic from paragraphs 136-137](data:image/png;base64,)

You can use the above diagram to calculate the size of any *halachic* measurement. For example, if you want to calculate how many eggs are in a קב, you would multiply 6 x 4 = 24, since there are 6 eggs in a לוג and 4 לוג in a קב. 

Regarding *hafrashas challah,* we learned above that the Gemara teaches that the measurement is 1/10 of an *eifah.* If we want to figure out that exact measurement in eggs, we would need to calculate how many eggs are in an *eifah* and take 10% of that. Using the above diagram, we can easily calculate the number of eggs in an *eifah* by multiplying 6 x 4 x 6 x 3 = 432 eggs. 10% of 432 is 43.2, meaning that the minimum amount of dough required for *hafrashas challah* is 43⅕ eggs.

However, there is another Gemara that can also shed light on the volume needed for *hafrashas challah.* The **גמרא פסחים** (קט.) (42) teaches that a *revi’is* (¼ of a לוג) is a volume of 2 fingerbreadths by 2 fingerbreadths by 2.7 fingerbreadths, which equals a total volume of **10.8 cubic fingerbreadths** (2 x 2 x 2.7) (see image). Thus, an entire לוג is 43.2 cubic fingerbreadths (10.8 x 4). Using the calculation above, we can calculate that there are 72 לוג in an *eifah* (4 x 6 x 3), which totals a volume of 3110.4 cubic fingerbreadths. Since the minimum amount of dough required for *challah* is 1/10 of an *eifah,* the volume required is 311.04 cubic fingerbreadths.

![Official diagram at paragraph 140](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

The S”A and *Rama* in **סימן שכד-א** (43) *passkin* like both of the above גמרות. The S”A writes that one is only obligated to be *mafrish challah* from a batch of dough made from the five grains, and only if it contains the volume of 43⅕ eggs. The **ש״ך** adds that an easy way to remember this is the word חלה, which has the *gematria* of 43, and the ה at the end also alludes to the additional ⅕. The S”A also references the טור (או״ח סימן תנ"ו), who explains that this volume can be measured by using the water-displacement method. A bowl is filled to the top with water and placed inside a bigger empty bowl. One then places 43⅕ eggs into the smaller bowl, and the amount of displaced water that overflows equals the volume of flour needed for *hafrashas challah*. 

The *Rama* adds, based on the second Gemara above, that this volume can also be calculated by constructing a *kli* with a volume of 10 fingerbreadths x 10 fingerbreadths and a height of 3 and ⅑  fingerbreadths (or 3.1111). The volume of such a vessel is 311 cubic fingerbreadths (10 x 10 x 3.111). The *Rama* concludes that the fingerbreadth referred to here is the width of an average thumb (see image above).
