blocks.text: III. The contradiction

At first glance, the two methods of calculation mentioned in the S”A appear to describe the same measurement and should therefore produce the same volume. However, the צל"ח (Rav Yechezkel Landau, 1713-1793, author of the נודע ביהודה) points out that, in practice, the two methods yield drastically different results. The צל״ח (פסחים קטז:) (44) writes that he measured both 43.2 eggs and 311 cubic thumb-widths and discovered that the thumb-widths calculation was almost double that of the egg-based calculation. The צל״ח had to do the actual calculation, but today by using ChatGPT, you can have it do the calculation for you.

At first glance, the two methods of calculation mentioned in the S”A appear to describe the same measurement and should therefore produce the same volume. However, the צל"ח (Rav Yechezkel Landau, 1713-1793, author of the נודע ביהודה) points out that, in practice, the two methods yield drastically different results. The **צל״ח** (פסחים קטז:) (44) writes that he measured both 43.2 eggs and 311 cubic thumb-widths and discovered that the thumb-widths calculation was almost double that of the egg-based calculation. The צל״ח had to do the actual calculation, but today by using ChatGPT, you can have it do the calculation for you.

We’ll first calculate the volume of 43.2 eggs and then the volume of 311 cubic thumbs. According to ChatGPT, the average volume of an egg is between 50-55 ml. Using an average volume of about 52 ml per egg, the volume of 43.2 eggs equals approximately 2246.4 ml (52 x 43.2), or about **2.25 liters**.

Now let’s calculate the thumb measurement. The average width of a male thumb is approximately 2.5 cm (also according to ChatGPT). If you make a vessel with the volume of 10 thumb-widths by 10 thumb-widths by 3 and ⅑thumb-widths, the vessel will hold **4.86 liters**, almost double the measurement of the eggs! This is a major discrepancy between the two measurements brought in the Gemara and employed in the *pssak* of the S”A and *Rama*!

blocks.text: The צל״ח concludes that one of two possibilities must be true: either the size of eggs has shrunk by approximately half or people’s thumbs have approximately doubled in size. Ultimately, he concludes that eggs have shrunk, and today’s eggs are approximately half the size of those used in Chazal’s calculations. Therefore, if one wishes to calculate the minimum size for hafrashas challah using today’s eggs, about 86 eggs would be required. The צל״ח adds that since our eggs are half the size of those used by Chazal, and a kezayis is half an egg, one of today’s eggs would be equal to one kezayis. Consequently, he would calculate the kezayis of matzah and maror to be used on Pesach as equal to the size of a modern-day egg.

chunks.contentMarkdown:
<u>IV. The צל״ח and חזון איש reconciliation</u>

The **צל״ח** concludes that one of two possibilities must be true: either the size of eggs has shrunk by approximately half or people’s thumbs have approximately doubled in size. Ultimately, he concludes that eggs have shrunk, and today’s eggs are approximately half the size of those used in Chazal’s calculations. Therefore, if one wishes to calculate the minimum size for *hafrashas challah* using today’s eggs, about 86 eggs would be required. The צל״ח adds that since our eggs are half the size of those used by Chazal, and a *kezayis* is half an egg, one of today’s eggs would be equal to one *kezayis.* Consequently, he would calculate the *kezayis* of *matzah* and *maror* to be used on Pesach as equal to the size of a modern-day egg.  

The **חזון איש** (או״ח לט-יב) (45) *passkins* like the צל״ח and writes that this was also the *pssak* of the **חתם סופר** and many others (including the גר״א quoted in the פת״ש (שכד-א)). The חזון איש also cites  the תשובה מאהבה, a student of the צל״ח, who describes the צל״ח as a very tall and large individual. The תשובה מאהבה suggested to his *rebbe* that maybe his measurements were inaccurate because he used his own thumbs, which were larger than average, and the צל״ח laughed in response, implying that perhaps he rescinded his *pssak*. 

The חזון איש, however, strongly rejects the possibility that the צל״ח retracted his *pssak* for a number of reasons: 1) The צל״ח was certainly aware that Chazal’s measurements were based on the thumb of an average person. 2) The תשובה מאהבה was not present when the actual measurements were being conducted. 3) Had the צל״ח really rescinded his *pssak,* he would have publicized it, since it is an earth-shattering *pssak* that has tremendous ramifications throughout *halacha*.

spans.text: V. Reconciliation of רב חיים נאה

blocks.text: In תש״ג (1943), רב חיים נאה published a sefer called שיעורי תורה where he argues on the צל״ח and maintains that the size of eggs has not decreased since the time of Chazal. In תש״ז (1947), the חזון איש responded by publishing קונטרס השיעורים to defend the position of the צל״ח. Two years later, in תש״ט (1949), the Steipler defended his brother-in-law, the חזון איש, in a sefer called שיעורין דאורייתא. Later that year, רב חיים נאה defended his opinion by publishing another sefer called שיעורי ציון. We could spend months going through the intricacies and back-and-forth arguments of this fundamental and far-reaching dispute, but we will only mention a few main points to help us better understand the various opinions.

blocks.text: VI. How do we passkin?

The ביאור הלכה (סימן רעא ד״ה יש רביעית) (47) quotes the צל״ח’s question regarding the large discrepancy between the thumb-based and egg-based measurements and writes that although the צל"ח asked “a great and difficult question,” there is an equally strong question on his answer from the גמרא יומא (פ.). The Gemara there writes that two cheekfuls of an average-sized man is slightly more than a revi’is, and a revi’is is about the size of one and a half eggs. Accordingly, today, when the eggs are half the size they used to be, a revi’is would be the size of three of our eggs. The חפץ חיים writes that he asked several average-sized individuals if they could fit three eggs in their mouth, and the most any of them were able to fit was two. (Furthermore, we cannot explain this discrepancy that three eggs do not fit in a person’s mouth by suggesting that people themselves have become smaller, because the צל״ח writes explicitly that human body size has remained unchanged since the time of Chazal).

<u>VI. How do we</u> *<u>passkin</u>*<u>?</u>

	The **ביאור הלכה** (סימן רעא ד״ה יש רביעית) (47) quotes the צל״ח’s question regarding the large discrepancy between the thumb-based and egg-based measurements and writes that although the צל"ח asked “a great and difficult question,” there is an equally strong question on his answer from the גמרא יומא (פ.). The Gemara there writes that two cheekfuls of an average-sized man is slightly more than a *revi’is,* and a *revi’is* is about the size of one and a half eggs. Accordingly, today, when the eggs are half the size they used to be, a *revi’is* would be the size of three of our eggs. The חפץ חיים writes that he asked several average-sized individuals if they could fit three eggs in their mouth, and the most any of them were able to fit was two. (Furthermore, we cannot explain this discrepancy that three eggs do not fit in a person’s mouth by suggesting that people themselves have become smaller, because the צל״ח writes explicitly that human body size has remained unchanged since the time of Chazal). 

	The ביאור הלכה concludes that since there is a dispute regarding how to calculate today’s *shiurim* and we are not fully certain who to follow, one should be stringent for **biblical** ***mitzvos*** to follow the larger measurement of the **צל״ח**, while for **rabbinic** ***mitzvos***, the smaller measurement may be used. For example, when fulfilling the biblical *mitzvah* of eating *matzah* on Pesach night or of eating a *kezayis* of bread on the first night of Sukkos in the *sukkah*, the larger measurement of the צל״ח should be used to calculate the size of the *kezayis,* and it should be the size of today’s *beitzah* (since, according to the S”A, a *kezayis* is half the size of a *beitzah,* and our eggs are half the size of what they used to be). Similarly, when reciting *kiddush* on Friday night (which is, at least on its most basic level, a biblical mitzvah),[31] the size of a *revi’is* should be calculated based on the bigger measurement of the צל״ח. However, the eating of the *afikomen,* which is rabbinic, may be calculated using the smaller measurement of half a *beitzah* of the eggs today. The **משנ״ב** (תפו- ק״א) in *hilchos Pesach* quotes this *pssak* from the ביאור הלכה.

	What emerges from this ruling of the ביאור הלכה is that since the *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah* today is rabbinic, the amount of flour needed should be calculated based on the volume of 43.2 of today’s eggs. On the other hand, one might argue that since the *mitzvah* of *hafrashas challah* (at least in *Eretz Yisrael*) is an especially stringent rabbinic commandment (as we learned above), and potentially biblical, perhaps the larger *shiur* should be used (similar to the *revi’is* for *kiddush*). 

In the next subsection we will answer two fundamental questions: 1) Regarding the amount of flour needed for *hafrashas challah, lema’ase,* do we follow the צל״ח or רב חיים נאה? 2) Why is it that today everyone uses weight to calculate the required amount of flour when until now, we have only discussed measurement by volume? In the next subsection, we will answer these questions. 

Source Notes

[31]:  Although we *passkin* that the obligation to recite *kiddush* on a cup of wine is rabbinic, it seems that the ביאור הלכה is claiming that since the biblical *mitzvah* is being fulfilled when using a cup, the *shiur* of the צל״ח should be used. There is a lengthy debate if one fulfills the biblical obligation of *kiddush* by reciting the *Amidah* in *shul,* and this seems to be a proof that the משנ״ב felt that you do not fulfill your biblical obligation of *kiddush* during *davening* in shul on Shabbos night.

blocks.text: It is clear from the Gemara and Rishonim that the amount of flour required for hafrashas challah (either 43.2 eggs or 311 cubic thumb-widths) is calculated in volume. Nevertheless, we find that the רמב״ם already converts this volume into a weight, and the S”A (43) quotes him as writing that the volume of 43.2 eggs is equivalent to the weight of 520 Egyptian dirhams (silver coins). The חזון איש (או״ח יב-ח) explains that it can only be converted into weight if that is established by the Chachmei Yisrael and becomes the accepted custom among עם ישראל (which is most likely based on the pssak of Chachmei Yisrael of the previous generation). The reason the measurement was converted to weight is because it is easier to calculate weight at home than volume. This is done by the Chachamim of each generation filling a container with a volume of 43.2 eggs with flour, weighing it, and using that weight as the standard for hafrashas challah.

blocks.text: To better understand how the volume is converted into weight, a brief introduction is required. The ratio between volume and weight depends on the density of the substance being measured. For water, the ratio of volume to weight is equal, such that one liter of water weighs 1 kg.[32] However, one liter of water weighs more than one liter of feathers because feathers are much less dense. Similarly, flour also weighs much less than water, with one liter of flour weighing about 0.5 kg. However, this measurement applies only when the flour is loosely poured into the container. If the flour is packed in tightly, more flour can fit in the same container with the same volume. Here the posskim write that tightly packed flour weighs approximately two-thirds as much as an equal volume of water. Thus, 1 liter of tightly packed flour weighs approximately .67 kg rather than .5 kg. This distinction is significant because there is a dispute in the Rishonim whether the volume of 43.2 eggs necessary for hafrashas challah is calculated based on packed flour or loosely poured flour. This obviously affects the amount of flour, and therefore the weight, needed in practice for hafrashas challah.

Thus, the shiur needed for challah is 2488 cc (57.6 x 43.2), or 2.48 liters. If flour weighs approximately half of its volume, the corresponding weight required for hafrashas challah would be 1.24 kg, which he rounds up to 1.25 kg. The שמירת שבת כהלכתה (פמ״ב-ט) writes that one should estimate even lower and be mafrish from flour weighing 1.2 kg. (It seems that the שש״כ is concerned that the ratio between the volume and weight of flour is not half, but 48% of the weight of water, and therefore he multiplies .48 x 2488, yielding 1.2). However, רב חיים נאה writes that one should not recite a bracha on this amount because according to some Rishonim, one should measure the volume with densely packed flour, which yields a much higher weight. Thus, the weight of 2488 cc of packed flour is two-thirds of that, which is 1658 cc, or 1.66 kg. Therefore, רב חיים נאה passkins that one should be mafrish without a bracha when using 1.25 kg of flour and recite a bracha when using at least 1.66 kg, at which point all opinions would require a bracha.

blocks.text: It is clear that Sephardim who follow Rav Ovadya should be mafrish with a bracha when using 1.56 kg, but how do Ashkenazim passkin? Do they passkin like רב חיים נאה or the חזון איש? The custom in Yerushalayim was to always passkin like רב חיים נאה (even for biblical commandments). Therefore, one should be mafrish with a bracha on 1.66 kg of flour. This is also the pssak of the שש״כ (מב-ט), RSZA in הליכות שלמה (פסח פ״ז-הע׳ 78), Rav Wosner in שבט הלוי (חי״א רנג-ג) and the minhag in Yerushalayim. Nevertheless, the Steipler and Rav Chaim Kanievsky are machmir like the חזון איש that a bracha is recited from only from 2.25 kg. This seems to be the accepted custom in the US, where a bracha is generally recited only when using 5 pounds (which is approximately equivalent to 2.25 kg) or more. However, it should be emphasized again that according to most opinions, one should be mafrish challah without a bracha when using 1.2 kg of flour.

For water, the ratio of volume to weight is equal, such that one liter of water weighs 1 kg.[32] However, one liter of water weighs more than one liter of feathers because feathers are much less dense. The **שמירת שבת כהלכתה** (פמ״ב-ט) writes that one should estimate even lower and be *mafrish* from flour weighing <u>1.2 kg</u>. (It seems that the שש״כ is concerned that the ratio between the volume and weight of flour is not half, but 48% of the weight of water, and therefore he multiplies .48 x 2488, yielding 1.2). However, רב חיים נאה writes that one should not recite a *bracha* on this amount because according to some *Rishonim,* one should measure the volume with densely packed flour, which yields a much higher weight. Thus, the weight of 2488 cc of packed flour is two-thirds of that, which is 1658 cc, or 1.66 kg. Therefore, רב חיים נאה *passkins* that one should be *mafrish* without a *bracha* when using 1.25 kg of flour and recite a *bracha* when using at least 1.66 kg, at which point all opinions would require a *bracha*.

Based on this, **Rav Ovadya Yosef** (49) in הליכות עולם (ח״א-עמ׳ רפח) initially writes that one should be *mafrish* with a *bracha* from 1.66 kg of dough. However, he then cites a *talmid chacham* who traveled to Egypt to examine historical dirhams from various periods, and he found that none ever weighed more than 3 grams. Therefore, Rav Ovadya concludes that one should be *mafrish* with a *bracha* from a batch of dough that weighs 1.56 kg (3 x 520). 

It is clear that *Sephardim* who follow Rav Ovadya should be *mafrish* with a *bracha* when using 1.56 kg, but how do *Ashkenazim passkin*? Do they *passkin* like רב חיים נאה or the חזון איש? The custom in Yerushalayim was to always *passkin* like רב חיים נאה (even for biblical commandments). Therefore, one should be *mafrish* with a *bracha* on **1.66 kg** of flour. This is also the *pssak* of the **שש״כ** (מב-ט), **RSZA** in הליכות שלמה (פסח פ״ז-הע׳ 78), **Rav Wosner** in שבט הלוי (חי״א רנג-ג) and the *minhag* in Yerushalayim. Nevertheless, the ***Steipler*** and **Rav Chaim Kanievsky** are *machmir* like the חזון איש that a *bracha* is recited from only from **2.25 kg**. This seems to be the accepted custom in the US*,* where a *bracha* is generally recited only when using 5 pounds (which is approximately equivalent to 2.25 kg) or more. However, it should be emphasized again that according to most opinions, one should be *mafrish challah* without a *bracha* when using 1.2 kg of flour. 

To summarize:

- **1.2 kg (2.65 lbs)** – Separate without a *bracha* according to most opinions

- **1.56 kg (3.44 lbs)** – **Rav Ovadya**: Separate with a *bracha*

- **1.66 kg (3.66 lbs)** – **רב חיים נאה**: Separate with a *bracha*

- **2.25 kg (4.96 lbs) – חזון איש**: Separate with a *bracha*

There are two last points that are important to stress: 1) The **חתם סופר** (או״ח קכז ד״ה או) and many others *passkin* that the above weight refers only to the flour itself, and not to the total weight after adding water, sugar and eggs. 2) As we will see in the next section, the weight calculations may vary depending on the type of flour being used. 

Source Notes

[32]:  We will use kilos when calculating weight since the metric system is the one generally used by *posskim* in this matter*.* Those living in the U.S., where pounds are used, can easily convert the measurements using the formula 1 kg = 2.2 lbs. 

[33]:  Rav Elyashiv in הליכות שדה (עמ׳ 134) explains that we do not need to be *machmir* for both the densely packed flour and the larger *shiur* of the חזו״א.

[34]:  There are many more opinions, but in the notes, we have quoted the three primary ones. Other opinions include the בן איש חי (שמיני שנה א) and Rav Mordechai Eliyahu in התורה והארץ (ח״ה) who require *hafrasha* without a *bracha* from 1.66 kg and with a *bracha* from 2.49 kg, and Rav Tuccachinsky in ספר ארץ ישראל (חלה-ב), who writes that one should be *mafrish* from 1.05 kg without a *bracha* and with a *bracha* from 1.57 kg.

Let’s explain. If 1.2 kg is really the amount needed for hafrashas challah, then there is no problem, because the batch of dough was already obligated and was exempted by your initial hafrasha, and the additional flour that was added later (which is less than 1.2 kg of flour) is not enough to require a new hafrasha. However, if 1.66 kg is the minimum amount required for hafrasha, your original hafrasha on 1.3 kg was meaningless. Once  you add enough flour to exceed the 1.66 kg threshold, the dough becomes obligated in hafrasha for the first time, and it should ideally be done with a bracha. In other words, if you ask the posskim/Rishonim who require hafrasha on 1.2 kg,[35] they would tell you that you do not need to be mafrish at all, but if you ask the posskim/Rishonim who hold that you need 1.66 kg,[36] they would tell you that you now have to be mafrish with a bracha.

### G. *Practical Applications*

In this section, we will delve further into the *halachos* that pertain to the amount of flour needed and apply what we learned in the previous section. As a reminder, we learned that if you are using **1.2 kg** of flour, everyone agrees you should be *mafrish* without a *bracha.* In order to recite a *bracha,* we saw three opinions in the *Acharonim*: **1.66** according to רב חיים נאה, **1.56** according to Rav Ovadya, and **2.25** kg according to the חזון איש*.* For the sake of clarity, in the subsections below we will use the measurement of רב חיים נאה, but the same principles apply according to the measurements of Rav Ovadya and the חזון איש. 

<u>Made a small batch of dough and added more</u>

	If you make a batch of dough using 1.3 kg of flour (an amount that most agree requires *hafrasha* without a *bracha*) and are *mafrish* without a *bracha,* you should be careful not to add enough flour afterward to bring the total amount to 1.66 kg or more – the amount that requires a *bracha* – since this creates a *safek* about whether you need to be *mafrish* again. Let’s explain. If 1.2 kg is really the amount needed for *hafrashas challah,* then there is no problem, because the batch of dough was already obligated and was exempted by your initial *hafrasha,* and the additional flour that was added later (which is less than 1.2 kg of flour) is not enough to require a new *hafrasha.* However, if 1.66 kg is the minimum amount required for *hafrasha*, your original *hafrasha* on 1.3 kg was meaningless. Once  you add enough flour to exceed the 1.66 kg threshold, the dough becomes obligated in *hafrasha* for the first time, and it should ideally be done with a *bracha.* In other words, if you ask the *posskim/Rishonim* who require *hafrasha* on 1.2 kg,[35] they would tell you that you do not need to be *mafrish* at all, but if you ask the *posskim/Rishonim* who hold that you need 1.66 kg,[36] they would tell you that you now have to be *mafrish* with a *bracha.* 

In essence, you are stuck. On the one hand, you cannot recite a *bracha* because perhaps this batch was already obligated and exempted by your original *hafrasha.* On the other hand, you also cannot eat the batch without being *mafrish*, since perhaps it has only now become obligated in *hafrasha* for the first time. It is therefore best to be *mafrish* again without a *bracha* (see קומץ החלה עמ׳ טז)*.*[37]

However, the **חלה כהלכתה** (סימן ה, שיח הלכה-י) (50) *passkins* that if the first batch was 1.3 kg and you were *mafrish* without a *bracha* (as required) and then you added another 1.3 kg, you should be *mafrish* again with a *bracha* ממה נפשך (regardless of which side is correct)*.* The logic is as follows: if the real requirement is 1.66, the *hafrasha* you did earlier on 1.3 kg was meaningless, and now that you have more than 1.66 for the first time, you should be *mafrish* with a *bracha.* On the flip side, if the real amount required to be *mafrish* is 1.2 kg, now that you have another 1.3, you should be *mafrish* and recite a *bracha.* Even though you were already *mafrish*, this side would say that since another 1.3 was added now, you should be *mafrish* again and recite a *bracha*. The only reason you did not recite a *bracha* earlier is because maybe the real requirement is 1.66 kg, but now, even that side would require you to recite a *bracha*, because for the first time, there is now more than 1.66. In other words, in this case, if you ask the *posskim/Rishonim* who hold you need 1.2 kg and the *posskim/Rishonim* who hold you need 1.66 kg, both would tell you to recite a *bracha.*

Source Notes

[35]:  Because they use loosely packed flour, as discussed in the previous section.

[36]:  Because they require densely packed flour.

[37]:  The לבוש מרדכי (חלה פ״ח-ט) writes that it is best to avoid adding the 1.3 kg after you were *mafrish,* lest you forget to be *mafrish* again. However, the חלה כהלכתה (סימן ה-ד) *passkins* that you are allowed to add more flour *le’chatchilla*, but you must be *mafrish m’safek* again since you added less than 1.2 kg.

blocks.text: Frozen flour

It is important to stress again that the measurement for hafrashas challah is based on volume, and the rishonim and later chachamim converted it into a measurement of weight. Therefore, the לבוש מרדכי (פ״ח-יא) (51) writes that since frozen flour weighs more than room temperature flour because it absorbs moisture when frozen, when using frozen flour, you should add a bit to the weight of 1.66 kg to ensure there is a volume of 43.2 eggs.

<u>Whole wheat</u> *<u>challah</u>*

![Official diagram at paragraph 180](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

In order to better understand this subsection, we first need to familiarize ourselves with the anatomy of the wheat kernel. A kernel is made up of three parts: the bran, the endosperm and the germ. The bran is the outer layer of the kernel, which makes up about 14% of it and is used when making whole wheat flour. The endosperm is the source of white flour and makes up about 83% of the kernel. The germ is the embryo – the sprouting section of the kernel, and makes up about 3% of the kernel. It is usually separated from the flour. Milling is the process of crushing the wheat kernel and separating it into its various parts. See video on the anatomy of a wheat kernel: [<u>bit.ly/SCPkernel</u>](https://bit.ly/SCPkernel) 

The S”A in **סימן שכד סעיף ג** (52) *passkins,* based on the **משנה חלה** (פ״ב-ו), that when calculating the volume of flour needed for *hafrashas challah*, the sourdough starter (שאור), bran (סובין) and wheat middling (מורסן), also known as the small pieces of bran, may be included in the calculation. However, if the bran is removed and later added back to the flour, it may not be included as part of the measurement. 

As shown in the video above, today most industrial mills first separate the white flour from the bran, and when they want to produce and sell whole wheat flour, they add the bran back.[38] This has major ramifications for *hafrashas challah.* If you make a batch of dough using 1.66 kg of whole wheat flour, you are still not allowed to recite a *bracha* when being *mafrish,* because the bran was added afterwards and may not be included in the required amount of flour. In such a situation, you must ensure that you have 1.66 kg of flour without the bran.

Based on the above, the **לבוש מרדכי** (פ״ח-יג) (53) writes that when buying whole wheat flour in which the bran is added back after milling, you need to add at least 15% to the required weight to ensure that you have the required amount of actual flour without the bran. Thus, according to רב חיים נאה, you may only be *mafrish* with a *bracha* if you have 1.916 kg of such whole wheat flour, and according to the חזון איש, only if you have 2.58 kg.[39]  

The לבוש מרדכי adds that if the bran was not removed during the milling process, as is common in smaller organic mills, then the required weight is actually less than 1.66 kg. Since the measurement for *hafrashas challah* is based on the volume of 43.2 eggs, and bran takes up more volume while weighing less than flour, a volume of 43.2 eggs filled with whole wheat flour will weigh less than the same volume filled with regular flour (1.66 kg). Therefore, when using proper whole wheat flour, in which the bran was never removed, the required weight will actually be less than the amounts listed above. 

The **לבוש מרדכי** writes that each of the 5 grains has a different weight when measured in a volume of 43.2 eggs. The weight also varies depending on whether the grain is whole or regular and whether the bran was removed and then added back to the flour or remained in the flour from the time of milling. The לבוש מרדכי measured and weighed each of the five grains, both whole grain (with bran, both when it was removed and later added back,[40] and when it remained in the flour throughout the milling[41]) and regular (without bran), and presents the findings in a neatly organized chart shown in the Marei Mekomos. 

Source Notes

[38]:  For this reason, you will see flour marketed as “80% whole wheat” or “50% whole wheat,” depending on how much bran they put back into the flour.

[39]:  It should be noted that the תשובות והנהגות (ח״ג-עא) *passkins* that since the bran was removed with intent to be added back, it is considered as if it was never removed. According to this, you only need to take into consideration the lighter weight and not the heavier one. Consequently, you may recite a *bracha* with 1.66 kg according to רב חיים נאה (or even from 1.59, since whole wheat flour weighs less than regular flour), even when using whole wheat flour.

blocks.text: Gluten-free wheat flour

We learned above in the משנה חלה (פ״א-א) (40) that hafrashas challah is compared to matzos on Pesach. Just as matzos may only be made from the five grains that can become chametz, so too, hafrashas challah is only required from flour made from those same five grains. Gluten is the ingredient that makes the flour rise, and today there are companies that produce wheat flour from which the  gluten has been removed. Is there an obligation to be mafrish challah from gluten-free wheat flour? On the one hand, gluten-free wheat flour does not fully rise and become chametz, but on the other hand, perhaps we look at wheat flour as a species: since ordinary wheat flour rises, even wheat flour from which the gluten has been removed is obligated in hafrashas challah.

chunks.contentMarkdown:
<u>Gluten-free wheat flour</u>

	We learned above in the **משנה חלה** (פ״א-א) (40) that *hafrashas challah* is compared to *matzos* on Pesach. Just as *matzos* may only be made from the five grains that can become *chametz*, so too, *hafrashas challah* is only required from flour made from those same five grains. Gluten is the ingredient that makes the flour rise, and today there are companies that produce wheat flour from which the  gluten has been removed*.* Is there an obligation to be *mafrish challah* from gluten-free wheat flour? On the one hand, gluten-free wheat flour does not fully rise and become *chametz,* but on the other hand, perhaps we look at wheat flour as a species: since ordinary wheat flour rises, even wheat flour from which the gluten has been removed is obligated in *hafrashas challah*. 

 The **אמרי יעקב** (ארץ ישראל ס״ב-ח ביאורים ד״ה ה׳ מיני דגן) (54) *passkins* that since there might be some remnants of gluten in the flour, one should be *mafrish* without a *bracha.* The **משנת יוסף** (חלק טו-רב) and the **אהל יעקב** (שכד-ז) also *passkin* that because of the *safek,* one should be *mafrish* without a *bracha.* However, Rav Rubin, the author of ארחות שבת, and the OU[42] *passkin* that in certain circumstances one should be *mafrish challah* with a *bracha.* 

In order to better understand this last question, we need to first understand how gluten-free wheat flour is made. In essence, gluten-free wheat flour is wheat starch. It is made by kneading flour and water into a batch of dough and then soaking the dough in water. The water becomes milky white because it absorbs the starch from the dough. The dough is then removed, and the remaining water sits until all the starch settles to the bottom, at which point the water is discarded and the starch is dried. Once dried, it is crushed and appears as white flour. See **video** for the exact process: <u>bit.ly/SCPglutenfreewheat</u>. Is this extract of flour considered “flour” that is obligated in *hafrasha*?

Rav Rubin writes that two main questions need to be answered: 1) If gluten is completely removed, do we say that since the flour cannot fully rise it is exempt from *challah,* or do we look at the species of flour and say that since ordinary wheat flour rises, this flour is also obligated in *hafrashas challah*?[43] 2) Even if we look at the species as a whole, perhaps *hafrashas challah* is only required when the entire grain, or at least the endosperm, is used, while  gluten-free flour is essentially just wheat starch (i.e., a derivative of flour). 

Regarding the first question, Rav Rubin in **היכלא** (חי״א-עמ׳ רכד) (55) quotes the ר״ן, who *passkins* that we look at the species of wheat flour as a whole. Since ordinary wheat flour rises, even if this specific flour does not, it is still obligated in *hafrashas challah.* Regarding the second question, Rav Rubin writes that according to the רי״ף, bread made with just the bran is considered bread even though it is missing the main ingredient of flour made from the endosperm. Although we do not *passkin* like the רי״ף regarding *matzah* on Pesach, we would still agree that wheat starch is considered flour regarding the obligation of *hafrashas challah,* since it is derived from the endosperm, the main part of the grain*.* 

Based on these two points, Rav Rubin *passkins* that one should be *mafrish challah* with a *bracha* on wheat starch. However, there is a caveat: if the wheat starch was made by non-Jews, a *bracha* should not be recited when being *mafrish.* This is based on the S”A in **של-א**, who *passkins* that flour owned and kneaded into dough by a non-Jew is not obligated in *challah.* Therefore, since the starch is produced by first kneading the flour into dough and then soaking it in water, if the initial kneading was done by a non-Jew, it was already exempt from *challah,* and no *hafrasha* is necessary*.* However, one may argue that since the non-Jew is not kneading the dough to make bread, it may not be considered “kneading by a non-Jew.” Therefore, it is best to be *mafrish* without a *bracha.* 

What emerges from here is that according to Rav Rubin, *hafrashas challah* with a *bracha* should be performed when making bread from wheat starch produced by a Jew, but if the starch was made by a non-Jew, a *bracha* should not be recited. Rav Rubin adds that today many gluten-free wheat flours  contain significant amounts of non-wheat additives, such as rice and corn flour. In order to be obligated in *hafrasha,* the volume of 43.2 eggs of the gluten-free wheat flour itself are necessary, without the other additives.[44] 

Furthermore, according to Rav Rubin, if the wheat starch is made into bread, the *bracha* is *hamotzi,* and if it is made into a pastry, the *bracha* is *mezonos.* The S”A in **או״ח סימן רח-ב** *passkins* that the *bracha* on a pastry made with the five grains and other ingredients is *mezonos,* even if the five grains are a minority, as long as the grains are not used as a binding agent. The **וזאת הברכה** (עמ׳ 201) writes that if “wheat starch” is listed after the main ingredient, such as corn flour, the wheat starch is being used as a binding agent, and the *bracha* on the food is *shehakol.* The example he gives is Cocoa Puffs, which has wheat starch listed as the second ingredient, and the *bracha* is *shehakol* because wheat starch is used as a binding agent. (According to the Star-K, when wheat comprises less than 15% of a product, it generally serves only as a binding agent. When it exceeds 25%, it also contributes flavor. Between 15% and 25%, its function is considered a *safek*, and the manufacturer should be contacted to clarify its intended purpose.)

chunks.title: Is Hafrashas Challah Biblical or Rabbinic?
chunks.summary: S”A: biblical in root, today biblical only in EY when Jewish people live there; chu”l is rabbinic so it will not be forgotten.
chunks.sectionTitle: Questions & Answers

blocks.text: Is the mitzvah of hafrashas challah biblical or rabbinic?

The S”A in סעיף א passkins that the mitzvah of hafrashas challah is biblical, but in סעיף ב he clarifies that it is only biblical in Eretz Yisrael when all of the Jewish people are living there. In סעיף ג, he adds that in chutz la’aretz, the mitzvah was rabbinically enacted so the mitzvah of challah will not be forgotten.

3. If the majority of Jews live in Israel, what will be the status of the upcoming *shemittah*? Will there be any room to rely on *heter mechira*? Is the *mitzvah* of *terumah* affected today?

Regarding *shemittah,* the **רמב״ם** (4) *passkins* that *shemittah* will only be a biblical obligation when *yovel* is biblically required. *Yovel* is only biblically required when the majority of the Jewish people enter the land of Israel and settle in their ancestral portion based on their *shevet.* Thus, only when *Mashiach* comes, reveals the *shevet* of each individual, and settles him in the appropriate area, will *shemittah* become biblical.

Regarding *terumah,* the **ראב״ד** (8) *passkins* that the obligation is biblical even without a majority of Jews living in the land. In contrast, the **רמב״ם** (8) equates it to *challah* and *passkins* that it will only become biblical when the majority of Jews live in Israel. The **חזון איש** (9) writes that as opposed to *hafrashas challah,* even the רמב״ם agrees that regarding *terumah,* as long as the majority of Jews enter the land of Israel, even without direction from a King or Navi, the *mitzvah* becomes biblical. However, **Rav Chaim Kanievsky** (10) suggests that since there are 10 lost tribes, even if all the Jews come to Israel today, the majority of Jews (i.e., the 10 lost tribes) are still in *chutz la’aretz,* and thus, *terumah* will remain rabbinic until *Mashiach* comes*.*

You are baking *matzah* with your *frum* friend and tell him, “I buy the *matzos* from which *challah* was not separated so my wife can make the *bracha* later.” He tells you, “That’s a ‘*frum* rookie’ mistake; you will forget to be *mafrish.*” He was right - What do you do when you remember on Pesach night? How is this case different than the *challah* on Shabbos?

If you live in *chu”l* and do not know which *matzah* came from which batch of dough, the **משנ״ב** (17) *passkins* that you should leave over a bit from each *matzah* and on *chol ha’moed* place all the pieces in a bowl and be *mafrish* from all of them. 

If you live in *EY,* there are three possible solutions: 1) **RSZA** (18) *passkins* that if there is no other way to get *matzah,* you are allowed to be *mafrish* in order to enable you to fulfill the biblical *mitzvah* of eating *matzah.* He adds that when being *mafrish* in *Eretz Yisrael* on Yom Tov, it is best to make the declaration mentally without verbalizing it and without reciting a *bracha* (but the physical separation still needs to be performed)*.*  2) The **חלת לחם**  (20) writes that you can give the *matzah* to a 12-year-old boy or 11-year-old girl who will be *mafrish challah.* This is permitted because at that age the *hafrasha* is valid, and according to the רשב״א, a *katan* is allowed to violate a rabbinic prohibition for his own sake. 3) **RSZA** (3) suggests that the  Rav of every community should be *mafrish challah* right before Pesach and have in mind that it should cover all those who forgot. See notes for more details.

blocks.text: True story: You wrap the challah with aluminum foil and burn it in your oven, but when you take it out, you notice that the dough rose and the foil ripped. Are you allowed to eat the other food that was baked in the oven at the same time? What about the rack it was on?

spans.text: with aluminum foil and burn it in your oven, but when you take it out, you notice that the dough rose and the foil ripped. Are you allowed to eat the other food that was baked in the oven at the same time? What about the rack it was on?

blocks.text: You are allowed to eat the other food that was baked in the oven since there is no issue ofריחא  or זיעה. Let’s explain. There is no issue of ריחא, since in a be’dieved situation (where the foods were already cooked together), reicha is not taken into consideration (see S”A יו"ד סימן ק"ח). There is also no issue of זיעה, since the dough is not a liquid and does not emit זיעה. Based on this, the חיי הלוי  (33) passkins that the other food in the oven is permitted. However, the rack which came in direct contact with the challah needs to be kashered. Some acharonim, such as the הפרשת חלה כהלכתה (עמ׳ קה), argue on Rav Moshe and passkin that even bread emits steam and all the food in the oven, as well as the oven itself, would be rendered not-kosher, if the foil rips.

blocks.text: You throw your hafrashas challah matzah into the biur chametz fire when your frum friend yells “Hey! You are ruining everything for us! We can’t burn our chametz here anymore!” What is he talking about?

blocks.text: The חלקת בנימין (34) asks that if one throws challah into the biur chametz, others should be forbidden from throwing their chametz in because they are benefitting from the extra flames created by the burning challah. chunks.title: Why Chazon Ish Shiurim Are Large
chunks.summary: Tzlach/Chazon Ish resolve discrepancy by saying eggs shrank; Rav Chaim Naeh reconciles differently.
chunks.sectionTitle: Questions & Answers

blocks.text: The חזון איש once promised that no missiles will ever fall in Bnei Brak. A few years ago, a fragment from a missile fell in the city. They quickly ran with it to Rav Chaim Kanievsky and asked “Look a missile fell! What happened to the promise of the חזון איש?” Rav Chaim looked at it and said, “It’s so small, it’s not the shiur of the חזון איש.” Why are the sizes of the חזון איש so large?

spans.text: The חזון איש once promised that no missiles will ever fall in Bnei Brak. A few years ago, a fragment from a missile fell in the city. They quickly ran with it to Rav Chaim Kanievsky and asked “Look a missile fell! What happened to the promise of the חזון איש?” Rav Chaim looked at it and said, “It’s so small, it’s not the
of the חזון איש.” Why are the sizes of the חזון איש so large?

blocks.text: The גמרא פסחים (42) teaches that the volume of a revi’is (1/4 of a לוג) is 2 fingerbreadths by 2 fingerbreadths by 2 and 7/10 fingerbreadths, which comes out to a volume of 10.8 cubic fingerbreadths (2x2x2.7). When using this calculation (where a fingerbreadth is 2.5 cm), the size of 1/10 of an eifah equals 4.86 liters. However, when using the average volume of an egg (52 cc), the volume of 1/10 of an eifah equals 2.25 liters! Therefore, the צל״ח (44) and theחזון איש  (45) conclude that the size of our eggs have shrunk almost in half. If the eggs of Chazal were double the size of eggs today, then the volumes mentioned in the two גמרות would be aligned. The צל״ח concludes that since a kezayis is half the size of an egg of Chazal, today’s kezayis is the size of our eggs. See, however, the notes for the reconciliation of רב חיים נאה.

chunks.contentMarkdown:
15. The חזון איש once promised that no missiles will ever fall in Bnei Brak. A few years ago, a fragment from a missile fell in the city. They quickly ran with it to Rav Chaim Kanievsky and asked “Look a missile fell! What happened to the promise of the חזון איש?” Rav Chaim looked at it and said, “It’s so small, it’s not the *shiur* of the חזון איש.” Why are the sizes of the חזון איש so large?

The **גמרא פסחים** (42) teaches that the volume of a *revi’is* (1/4 of a לוג) is 2 fingerbreadths by 2 fingerbreadths by 2 and 7/10 fingerbreadths, which comes out to a volume of **10.8 cubic fingerbreadths** (2x2x2.7). When using this calculation (where a fingerbreadth is 2.5 cm), the size of 1/10 of an *eifah* equals 4.86 liters. However, when using the average volume of an egg (52 cc), the volume of 1/10 of an *eifah* equals 2.25 liters! Therefore, the **צל״ח** (44) and the**חזון איש**  (45) conclude that the size of our eggs have shrunk almost in half. If the eggs of Chazal were double the size of eggs today, then the volumes mentioned in the two גמרות would be aligned. The צל״ח concludes that since a *kezayis* is half the size of an egg of Chazal, today’s *kezayis* is the size of our eggs. See, however, the notes for the reconciliation of רב חיים נאה.

16. It’s the *seder* night and you are about to eat *matzah*. Your son asks you, “Do we *passkin* like the חזון איש? How much *matzah* should I eat?” What do you answer?

The **ביאור הלכה** (47) *passkins* that for biblical *mitzvos,* one should follow the calculation of the צל״ח. Therefore, for the first *kezayis* of *matzah,* one should use the larger *shiur,* but one is not required to use that measurement for the *afikomen,* which is rabbinic. The custom in Yerushalayim, however, was always to follow the measurements of רב חיים נאה.

17. True story: Your wife made a batch of dough with 1.5 kg of flour and was *mafrish challah,* when your neighbors called, asking if they could come with their family for Shabbos lunch. She agrees and quickly adds another kg of flour, more water, and mixes everything together. Is she obligated to be *mafrish* again?

She should be *mafrish* without a *bracha*. Let’s explain. If 1.2 kg is really the amount needed for *hafrashas challah,* then the first batch of dough was already obligated and exempted by the *hafrasha*, while the additional flour added now (which is less than 1.2 kg) is not enough to require a new *hafrasha.* However, if 1.66 kg is the amount needed to be *mafrish*, then the *hafrasha* you made on the 1.2 kg is not valid, and when you now add more flour and exceed the 1.66 kg threshold, you are obligated to be *mafrish* for the first time, which should ideally be with a *bracha.* Therefore, it is best to avoid this situation, but when it is necessary to do so, you should be *mafrish* again without a *bracha.*

chunks.title: Frozen Flour Needs More Weight
chunks.summary: Frozen flour absorbs moisture and may weigh more than its real flour volume.
chunks.sectionTitle: Questions & Answers

blocks.text: You perfectly weigh the exact amount of flour needed to recite the bracha for hafrashas challah, when your daughter in seminary says, “I heard that if you take the flour out of the freezer, you need to add more flour!” What is she talking about?

spans.text: You perfectly weigh the exact amount of flour needed to recite the
when your daughter in seminary says, “I heard that if you take the flour out of the freezer, you need to add more flour!” What is she talking about?

blocks.text: Theלבוש מרדכי  (51) writes that since frozen flour often absorbs moisture when frozen, it weighs more. Thus, if you use exactly 1.66 kg of flour, you are really using less than the volume of 43.2 eggs. Therefore, whenever using frozen flour, you should add a bit more flour to ensure that you have the required amount of flour that is equivalent to the volume of 43.2 eggs.

The**לבוש מרדכי**  (51) writes that since frozen flour often absorbs moisture when frozen, it weighs more. Thus, if you use exactly 1.66 kg of flour, you are really using less than the volume of 43.2 eggs. Therefore, whenever using frozen flour, you should add a bit more flour to ensure that you have the required amount of flour that is equivalent to the volume of 43.2 eggs.

chunks.title: Whole Wheat Needs More Flour
chunks.summary: Bran added back after milling may not count toward the 1.66 kg flour amount; may need about 1.9 kg.
chunks.sectionTitle: Questions & Answers

blocks.text: Your challah last Shabbos was so great that you decide this week to try making whole wheat challah. This time, to be safe, you weigh 1.8 kg of flour, but when you tell your frum friend what you are doing, he yells “Hey! You need more flour than that! It’s whole wheat!” What is he talking about?

friend what you are doing, he yells “Hey! You need more flour than that! It’s whole wheat!” What is he talking about?

blocks.text: The S”A (52) passkins that if you remove the bran from the flour and add it back later, the bran cannot be included in the calculation of 1.66 kg. Today, most mills selling whole wheat flour indeed remove the bran and then add it again later. Therefore, when using whole wheat flour to bake bread, you will need 1.9 kg of flour, of which there is 1.66 kg of flour obligated in hafrasha. See notes for more details.

chunks.title: Gluten-Free Wheat Flour
chunks.summary: Some say separate without bracha; Rav Rubin requires with bracha in certain Jewish-produced wheat-starch cases.
chunks.sectionTitle: Questions & Answers

blocks.text: Are you obligated to be mafrish challah on gluten-free wheat flour?

The אמרי יעקב (54) passkins that since gluten-free wheat flour cannot become chametz, it should really be exempt from hafrasha, but since some gluten always enters into the flour, you should be mafrish without a bracha. Rav Rubin (55) passkins that if the flour is made by Jews, you are mafrish with a bracha (assuming you have 1.66 kg of actual wheat flour), but if it is made by non-Jews, you should be mafrish without a bracha. See notes for details.

You are already a mini-master in the *halachos* of *hafrashas challah,* so your wife asks you: “Since we are not having guests this week, I made challah with 1 kg of flour, but the yeast went crazy and the dough rose to a size much greater than 43.2 eggs.
